title: A laboratory without weight
statement: A small freely falling laboratory recovers the local physics of special relativity.

title: Universality and local physics
body: The weak equivalence principle states that ideal test bodies released at the same event with the same velocity fall alike, independently of composition. In Newtonian language their acceleration is \(\mathbf a=(m_g/m_i)\mathbf g\); universality makes the ratio common, and a choice of mass units sets \(m_g\overset{\text{mass convention}}{=}m_i\). This equality compares gravitational response with inertial resistance, not two separately derived formulas.
statement: Ideal test bodies with the same initial position and velocity fall alike, independently of composition.

title: The Einstein principle
body:
The weak equivalence principle concerns the trajectories of test bodies. The Einstein equivalence principle goes further: local nongravitational experiments in a freely falling, nonrotating laboratory should obey special relativity, independently of the laboratory's location and velocity.

This is why free fall is useful for more than dropping objects. It also tells us how to interpret local clocks, light signals and electromagnetic experiments. The reference is to \cref{inertial physical laws}{sr.principle_of_relativity}, now recovered locally rather than throughout a whole curved region.

An accelerating laboratory in flat spacetime can reproduce the feeling of weight. Consequently, feeling weight alone does not establish that spacetime is curved; comparing separated free-fall experiments is a different test.
statement: Local nongravitational laws have their SR form in a freely falling, nonrotating laboratory.

title: What a falling experiment tests
body: Release two small bodies beside an accelerometer inside a freely falling capsule. Neglect air drag, charge forces, spin effects and their own gravity. Locally they float together. Repeat the experiment with a larger separation and sensitive instruments: converging or diverging trajectories reveal \cref{tidal gravity}{gr.tidal_gravity}. Equal free-fall response does not imply equal motion for bodies subject to different nongravitational forces.
statement: Increasing a falling experiment’s size can reveal tidal differences that a point laboratory misses.

title: What the principle does not prove
body: The equivalence principle motivates a metric description, but does not by itself derive Einstein's field equations. Nor can it remove curvature over a finite laboratory. Strong-equivalence statements involving self-gravitating bodies are stronger than the local nongravitational principle used here. See \cref{local inertial frames}{gr.local_inertial_frame} for its coordinate expression.
statement: The equivalence principle neither removes tidal gravity nor uniquely determines gravitational field equations.

title: Coordinates adapted to free fall
body:
In special relativity an inertial frame can cover a whole flat region. Near a gravitating body, however, two separated free-fall laboratories can change their separation even though neither feels a force. We should therefore expect an inertial description to work locally, without assuming it works throughout the entire region.

A local inertial frame makes the coordinates agree with the measurements of one freely falling observer at one event. The \cref{equivalence principle}{gr.equivalence_principle.authored_3} supplies the physical interpretation: local nongravitational experiments have their SR form there. It does not say that distant laboratories share a single inertial frame.
statement: At a regular event, coordinates can match a freely falling observer’s inertial measurements.

title: The conditions at an event
body:
Choose coordinates centred on a regular event \(p\), using an orthonormal basis and the signature \(+---\). Local inertial coordinates satisfy
\[ egin{aligned}g_{\mu
u}(p)&=\eta_{\mu
u},\ \partial_ho g_{\mu
u}(p)&=0.\end{aligned}\]
The first condition fixes the measuring rule at the event. The second removes its first-order coordinate variation there, so the Levi-Civita connection coefficients vanish at \(p\). These are coordinate conditions, not field equations or a claim that curvature vanishes.
statement: Local inertial coordinates have Minkowski metric and vanishing first metric derivatives at their origin.

title: A point is not a region
statement: Removing first-order coordinate effects leaves second-order, curvature-dependent departures from SR.

title: Free fall and hovering
body: A coasting astronaut can carry a nonrotating local frame whose accelerometer reads zero. A hovering astronaut must fire a rocket and has nonzero proper acceleration, even if their spatial coordinates stay fixed. Being momentarily at rest in some coordinates is therefore not the criterion for an inertial laboratory.
statement: Coasting and hovering can share an instantaneous rest position but have different accelerometer readings.

title: Orthonormal is not automatically inertial
body: Making the metric Minkowskian at one point fixes the basis there; eliminating first derivatives also constrains how coordinates extend nearby. An accelerated observer has an instantaneous orthonormal frame but not an inertial laboratory over time. \cref{Local flatness}{gr.local_flatness} states the geometric result; the \cref{equivalence principle}{gr.equivalence_principle} connects it to physical experiments.
statement: An orthonormal basis at one event does not by itself make an accelerated laboratory inertial.

title: The observer's accelerometer
body:
An orbiting spacecraft and a dropped capsule are both examples of free fall. The spacecraft need not be falling straight downward; what matters is that it is not being pushed away from its natural trajectory by a nongravitational force.

Represent the observer by a \cref{timelike worldline}{math.worldline}. In the local inertial laboratory associated with that worldline, a small accelerometer reads zero. Earth-based coordinates may still show a large acceleration. These statements are compatible because one concerns a carried instrument and the other concerns position relative to a coordinate grid.
statement: Free fall is identified by zero proper acceleration, rather than zero coordinate acceleration.

title: A timelike geodesic observer
body:
A freely falling observer follows a timelike worldline with tangent \(u^\mu\coloneqq dx^\mu/d	au\). In the test-body approximation its covariant acceleration obeys \[a^\mu\coloneqq u^
u
abla_
u u^\mu\overset{	ext{free fall}}{=}0.\] Proper time \(	au\) is the observer's clock time. The first relation defines acceleration geometrically; the second imposes the force-free motion law.
statement: An ideal free-fall observer follows a timelike worldline with vanishing covariant acceleration.

title: Coordinate acceleration can remain
body:
Write the observer's tangent as \(u^\mu=dx^\mu/d\tau\), where \(\tau\) is the carried clock's time. Its physical four-acceleration is
\[a^\mu=\frac{du^\mu}{d\tau}+\Gamma^\mu{}_{\alpha\beta}u^\alpha u^\beta.\]
The first term describes changing components. The second corrects for how the coordinate basis changes along the path. Free fall sets their sum to zero; it does not require each term to vanish separately.

In a \cref{local inertial frame}{gr.local_inertial_frame.definition} the connection term vanishes at the chosen event, so free fall has the familiar inertial form there. In a ground-based chart it need not vanish. This is the mathematical reason that a falling capsule can speed up while its accelerometer remains at zero.
statement: The connection accounts for coordinate-basis changes, allowing a curved coordinate track with zero proper acceleration.

title: Weight on a surface
body: A person standing on a surface is held away from a free-fall trajectory by the ground's contact force. Their accelerometer reads a nonzero value. Conversely, an orbiting astronaut can feel weightless while the spacetime curvature produces measurable tidal acceleration between separated parts of the spacecraft.
statement: A surface or rocket supplies the proper acceleration that keeps an observer away from free fall.

title: Limits of the ideal observer
body: Treat the observer as small enough that spin, finite size, radiation reaction and self-gravity do not alter the test-particle motion. The geodesic model is an approximation for real extended bodies. Compare \cref{four-acceleration}{gr.four_acceleration} and \cref{tidal gravity}{gr.tidal_gravity}: zero acceleration of one ideal observer does not mean zero relative acceleration of neighbouring observers.
statement: Geodesic motion idealises a small test body whose size, spin and self-gravity can be neglected.

title: Compare neighbouring falls
statement: Relative acceleration of neighbouring free-fall trajectories reveals gravity that one falling frame cannot remove.

title: Relative acceleration
body: In the Newtonian limit let \(\mathbf g\coloneqq-\boldsymbol\nabla\Phi\), where \(\Phi\) is gravitational potential. Two nearby test bodies separated by \(\xi^j\) have \[\delta a^i\simeq-\partial_i\partial_j\Phi\,\xi^j.\] The approximation retains first order in separation. A uniform acceleration removes the gradient of the potential at a point, but not this Hessian.
statement: In the Newtonian limit, the potential’s second spatial derivatives give tidal relative acceleration.

title: Stretching and squeezing
body:
For a point mass, \(\Phi\coloneqq-GM/r\). A small radial separation has relative outward acceleration \(\delta a_r\simeq(2GM/r^3)\xi_r\): the inner body falls inward faster. A transverse separation is squeezed with coefficient \(-GM/r^3\). This comparison assumes separation much smaller than the radius and slow motion in a weak field.

\explanation{radial-coefficient}{Where does the radial stretching factor come from?}{The radial acceleration is \(g_r=-GM/r^2\). Differentiating gives \(dg_r/dr=2GM/r^3\), so two radii separated by a small \(\xi_r\) have acceleration difference \(2GM\xi_r/r^3\). The positive difference means the outer body accelerates inward less strongly than the inner one.}
statement: An isolated spherical mass stretches a small radial separation and squeezes transverse separations.

title: Curvature is the relativistic refinement
body: In GR the \cref{geodesic deviation equation}{gr.geodesic_deviation} replaces the potential Hessian by components of the Riemann tensor measured in the observer's frame. It compares a family of freely falling trajectories, rather than assigning a gravitational force to one trajectory. Vacuum outside a body can have tides even though its matter density vanishes.
statement: Geodesic deviation replaces the Newtonian tidal Hessian by relativistic curvature components.

title: Relative velocity is not enough
body: Two inertial particles can separate at constant relative velocity in flat spacetime. That alone is not a tidal effect. The curvature measurement concerns relative acceleration after controlling initial conditions and accounting for the observer's frame. A picture of diverging paths must be read with that qualification.
statement: Relative drift alone is not evidence of curvature; tidal tests concern relative acceleration.

title: Gravity changes the measuring structure
body: Special relativity studies matter on a fixed Minkowski geometry. General relativity makes geometry dynamical: the metric determines clock readings and causal directions, while its curvature and evolution respond to matter and boundary or initial data. Gravity concerns spacetime, not merely the shape of three-dimensional space.
statement: GR makes the metric a physical field governing measurements and responding to gravitational dynamics.

title: Two linked laws
body: The geometric description has two parts. Ideal test bodies follow the metric's timelike or null geodesics. The metric itself obeys gravitational field equations. The \cref{equivalence principle}{gr.equivalence_principle} motivates the first part and the local recovery of SR; it does not uniquely select the second.
statement: The geometric theory combines natural free-fall paths with a dynamical law for the spacetime metric.

title: From local freedom to finite-region effects
body:
The \cref{equivalence principle}{gr.equivalence_principle.authored_3} says that a sufficiently small freely falling laboratory recovers special relativity. This suggests treating free fall as natural motion, rather than as motion caused by a composition-dependent force in a preferred background frame.

But \cref{tidal experiments}{gr.tidal_gravity.overview} show that different nearby laboratories cannot generally be combined into one inertial frame over a finite region. We need geometry that is Minkowskian locally yet can curve across the region. A spacetime metric supplies exactly this kind of measuring structure.

This argument motivates the geometric description; it is not a uniqueness proof. A further physical law must determine how the metric responds to matter. Einstein's field equations supply that law in GR.

\explanation{space-versus-spacetime}{Is it just space that is curved?}{No. The metric also determines elapsed clock time and the directions light can follow. A picture of a curved spatial surface can help with one aspect of the geometry, but it omits the temporal part that is essential to gravitational motion and redshift.}
statement: Universal free fall motivates local inertial motion; persistent tides motivate curvature.

title: A curved metric is not a rubber sheet
body: A rubber-sheet model suggests a mass pulling objects downward through an external gravitational field. GR needs no embedding space or additional downward force. Even clock-rate differences belong to the metric, and light follows null paths without possessing rest mass. Curved coordinate lines alone also prove nothing: flat spacetime can be written in curvilinear coordinates.
statement: A rubber sheet omits time and requires an external force, so it is only a limited analogy.

title: Measurement, transport, curvature and dynamics
body: The \cref{spacetime metric}{gr.metric_tensor} explains measurement, connections explain comparison between neighbouring events, curvature describes the obstruction to flattening a region, and field equations supply dynamics. These are related but distinct questions. Matter is a source of curvature, but curvature can also persist and propagate in vacuum; the slogan must not imply that every curved region contains matter.
statement: Measurement, comparison, curvature and field dynamics are distinct parts of the geometric theory.

title: A field that measures intervals
body:
A coordinate grid tells us where an event is labelled, but not what a clock or ruler will measure there. The metric provides that missing information. It assigns a scalar product to tangent vectors at each event, allowing us to distinguish temporal, spatial and lightlike directions.

In SR one can use a fixed Minkowski metric throughout inertial Cartesian coordinates. In GR the same measuring role is played by a field \(g_{\mu\nu}(x)\). Its components may vary across spacetime, and the field itself participates in gravitational dynamics.

The \cref{tensor transformation law}{math.tensor_transformation_law} ensures that changing the grid changes the components without changing a measurement. A \cref{local inertial frame}{gr.local_inertial_frame.definition} then explains how the field recovers the Minkowski measuring rule at one event.
statement: A spacetime metric pairs local tangent vectors and determines intervals and causal directions.

title: A Lorentzian bilinear form
body:
The metric is a symmetric, nondegenerate covariant tensor \(g_{\mu
u}\) of signature \(+---\). For tangent vectors define \[g(V,W)\coloneqq g_{\mu
u}V^\mu W^
u.\] This contraction is coordinate-independent even though its components change. Nondegenerate means an inverse exists, not that every nonzero vector has nonzero norm: null vectors are essential.
statement: The metric is a symmetric, nondegenerate rank-(0,2) tensor field with signature \(+---\).

title: Read the line element
body:
With \(x^0\coloneqq ct\), the quadratic expression \(ds^2\coloneqq g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu\) has dimensions of length squared. In a chart with cross terms the coefficient of \(dt\,dr\) is twice the corresponding symmetric metric component when the coordinates themselves are \((t,r,\ldots)\). Always identify the coordinate convention before extracting components.

\explanation{cross-term}{Why does a cross term have a factor of two?}{The sum contains both \(g_{tr}\,dt\,dr\) and \(g_{rt}\,dr\,dt\). Symmetry gives \(g_{tr}=g_{rt}\), so together they contribute \(2g_{tr}\,dt\,dr\). Thus a coefficient \(B\) multiplying \(dt\,dr\) corresponds to \(g_{tr}=B/2\), not \(B\).}
statement: Contracting the metric with two infinitesimal displacements gives the line element.

title: Varying components without curvature
body: Flat spacetime in spherical spatial coordinates has \(ds^2=c^2dt^2-dr^2-r^2d\theta^2-r^2\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\). Its components depend on position, but the spacetime is flat. Conversely a curved spacetime can have Minkowski components at one event in a local inertial chart. Derivatives and their invariant combinations distinguish these cases.
statement: Position-dependent metric components can describe flat spacetime in curvilinear coordinates.

title: A field is more than a coordinate grid
body: The \cref{SR metric}{sr.metric_tensor} describes flat-spacetime measurement. Here the metric is a dynamical field; the \cref{inverse metric}{gr.inverse_metric}, \cref{line element}{gr.line_element} and curvature concepts develop its uses. In general the full metric cannot be made constant across a finite region by choosing better coordinates.
statement: A varying metric component is not itself a curvature measurement.

title: Returning from covectors to vectors
body: The metric converts a tangent vector into a covector. Its inverse reverses that conversion and allows contractions between covariant quantities. This is a matrix inverse in coordinates, not the reciprocal of every component.
statement: The inverse metric reverses lowering an index and converts covectors back into vectors.

title: The inverse relation
body:
Define \(g^{\mu
u}\) by \[g^{\mu\alpha}g_{\alpha
u}\overset{	ext{inverse definition}}{=}\delta^\mu{}_{
u}.\] The Kronecker delta represents the identity map. The superscripts indicate a contravariant tensor; they are not decorative labels on the same numerical array.
statement: The matrix inverse \(g^{\mu\alpha}g_{\alpha\nu}=\delta^\mu{}_{\nu}\) defines the inverse metric.

title: Raise and lower indices
body:
For a covector \(w_
u\), define \(w^\mu\coloneqq g^{\mu
u}w_
u\). Lowering again gives \(g_{ho\mu}w^\mu\overset{	ext{inverse metric}}{=}w_ho\). The equality uses the inverse relation. Raising one index on a rank-two tensor similarly changes its type and often the signs of its components; preserve which index was raised.

\explanation{index-roundtrip}{Follow one index through the round trip}{Starting with \(w_
u\), substitute the raising rule into the lowering rule:
\[ egin{aligned}g_{ho\mu}w^\mu&=g_{ho\mu}g^{\mu
u}w_
u\ &=\delta_ho{}^

u=w_ho.\end{aligned}\]
The repeated indices are summed. The free index \(ho\) identifies the component that survives.}
statement: Raising then lowering an index returns the original components because the metrics are inverse maps.

title: A diagonal coordinate metric
body: For the \(t,r\) sector \(ds^2=f(r)c^2dt^2-f(r)^{-1}dr^2\), the inverse entries are \(g^{tt}=1/(fc^2)\) and \(g^{rr}=-f\) wherever that chart is nonsingular. A diagonal matrix permits reciprocals of diagonal entries. Cross terms require inversion of the whole matrix, and a coordinate singularity should not be mistaken for a physically degenerate spacetime metric.
statement: Reciprocating diagonal entries works only when the coordinate metric is diagonal and nonsingular.

title: Different objects at different points
body: Use the metric and inverse at the same event. A vector at one event and a covector at another cannot be contracted without a rule for comparing tangent spaces. That comparison belongs to \cref{parallel transport}{gr.parallel_transport}; algebraic index movement is a separate operation.
statement: Index movement compares tensors at the same event; comparing different events requires extra structure.

title: Integrating physical volume
body:
Imagine integrating a scalar field over a region. Merely multiplying its value by \(dx^0dx^1dx^2dx^3\) would make the result depend on how finely we stretched the coordinate grid. The coordinate box is a box of labels, not yet a physical four-volume.

The metric tells us the physical scale and skewness of the coordinate directions. Its determinant combines those effects into a single factor, \(\sqrt{-g}\). Multiplying by that factor compensates for the change in coordinate box size.

This joins two inputs: the metric supplies measurement, while the \cref{coordinate transition}{math.coordinate_transformation} tells us how labels and their integration widths change. The cancellation is what makes a covariant action independent of the chosen chart.
statement: The metric determinant converts coordinate integration boxes into an invariant spacetime measure.

title: The invariant measure
body: Write \(g\coloneqq\det(g_{\mu\nu})\). In a nonsingular four-dimensional Lorentzian chart define \[dV_4\coloneqq\sqrt{|g|}\,d^4x=\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x.\] The last equality uses the negative determinant of a Lorentzian metric with one positive and three negative eigenvalues. This is the positive integration density; an oriented volume form additionally fixes orientation.
statement: In a regular Lorentzian chart, \(dV_4=\sqrt{-\det g_{\mu\nu}}\,d^4x\).

title: Why the Jacobian cancels
body:
Under a coordinate change let \(J\coloneqq\det(\partial x'/\partial x)\). The tensor transformation law gives \(g'=g/J^2\), while coordinate volume changes by \(d^4x'=|J|d^4x\). Consequently \(\sqrt{|g'|}d^4x'\overset{\text{Jacobian cancellation}}{=}\sqrt{|g|}d^4x\). Neither factor alone is invariant.

\explanation{determinant-square}{Why does the Jacobian appear squared?}{A metric has two covariant indices, so its matrix transformation has one inverse coordinate Jacobian on each side. Taking determinants multiplies by the inverse determinant twice: \(g'=g/J^2\). Taking the positive square root leaves \(1/|J|\), exactly what the integration measure needs.}
statement: The determinant’s inverse Jacobian factor exactly cancels the coordinate volume’s Jacobian.

title: Spherical coordinates in flat spacetime
body: Using coordinates \((ct,r,\theta,\phi)\), the flat metric has determinant \(-r^4\sin^2\theta\). Thus \(dV_4=r^2\sin\theta\,d(ct)\,dr\,d\theta\,d\phi\) on the usual angular chart. The familiar spherical factor arises without curvature. If the time coordinate is \(t\), the metric determinant supplies the extra factor of \(c\).
statement: The spherical factor \(r^2\sin\theta\) comes from the metric even in flat spacetime.

title: Spacetime and spatial volume differ
body: A three-dimensional slice uses its induced spatial metric and a three-volume element, not simply the four-dimensional determinant with \(dt\) erased. The four-volume element belongs in covariant actions such as the \cref{Einstein-Hilbert action}{gr.einstein_hilbert_action}. A vanishing coordinate determinant at a polar axis may signal a failed chart rather than a failed geometry.
statement: Spatial slice volume uses an induced three-metric, rather than simply deleting \(dt\) from four-volume.

title: Turn a metric into a clock or ruler
body: The line element is the metric evaluated on an infinitesimal displacement. It packages the coordinate components into a quadratic expression that can be integrated along an appropriate curve. It is not generally a formula for finite coordinate differences between distant events.
statement: The line element evaluates the metric on an infinitesimal displacement, rather than a finite endpoint difference.

title: The quadratic interval
body: Define \[ds^2\coloneqq g_{\mu\nu}(x)dx^\mu dx^\nu.\] With signature \(+---\), timelike displacements have positive squared interval, null displacements zero, and spacelike displacements negative. Along a timelike curve an ideal clock measures \(d\tau\coloneqq\sqrt{ds^2}/c\). For a spacelike curve its positive length element is \(d\ell\coloneqq\sqrt{-ds^2}\).
statement: The sign of \(ds^2=g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu\) distinguishes timelike, null and spacelike displacements.

title: Pull back to a curve
body:
For \(x^\mu(\lambda)\), insert \(dx^\mu=\dot x^\mu d\lambda\). The proper-time integral is \[\Delta\tau\coloneqq\frac1c\int\sqrt{g_{\mu\nu}(x(\lambda))\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu}\,d\lambda.\] A monotonic change of parameter changes both the tangent and integration element, leaving the result unchanged. The path itself, however, matters.

\explanation{parameter-cancellation}{Why does the parameter not affect the clock reading?}{Under an increasing relabelling \(\lambda\mapsto\lambda'\), each tangent gains a factor \(d\lambda/d\lambda'\). The square root of the quadratic form gains that factor once, which cancels the inverse factor in \(d\lambda'\). The same geometric path therefore gives the same elapsed clock time.}
statement: Substituting a curve’s tangent into the metric gives its parameter-independent proper-time integral.

title: Coordinate speed versus measured speed
body: For a radial null displacement in \(ds^2=fc^2dt^2-f^{-1}dr^2\), the null condition gives \(|dr/dt|\overset{\text{radial null}}{=}cf\). This coordinate speed need not equal \(c\). Outside the horizon a local static observer uses \(d\ell=dr/\sqrt f\) and \(d\tau=\sqrt f\,dt\), recovering \(|d\ell/d\tau|=c\).
statement: A position-dependent coordinate speed of light is compatible with every local measurement giving \(c\).

title: Do not replace differentials by differences
body: If the metric varies along a path, substituting endpoint coordinate differences into a metric evaluated at one endpoint does not compute elapsed proper time. Integrate along the actual worldline. For large separations even the choice and existence of connecting geodesics can be nontrivial.
statement: Elapsed time requires a path integral when the metric varies; endpoint differences alone do not suffice.

title: The time carried by a worldline
body:
Two clocks can meet, separate, and meet again. Agreement about the departure and reunion events does not require agreement about elapsed time, because the clocks have followed different histories.

The \cref{line element}{gr.line_element.definition} supplies the small proper-time increment at each point of a timelike worldline. Adding these increments along the actual path gives the clock reading. This combines a local measuring rule with a complete history; neither endpoint coordinate time nor a straight line on a coordinate picture can replace that history.

A freely falling clock is not required for this definition. An accelerated ideal clock also measures proper time (assuming its mechanism is not disturbed by acceleration); free fall concerns which path the clock follows.
statement: Proper time is the elapsed reading of an ideal clock along its particular timelike history.

title: Clock time from the metric
body: For a future-directed timelike curve define \[\Delta\tau\coloneqq\frac1c\int\sqrt{g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu}.\] The expression uses the \(+---\) convention. It is independent of coordinates; a coordinate time \(t\) equals the clock reading only in appropriately chosen circumstances.
statement: For a future-directed timelike path, \(\Delta\tau=c^{-1}\int\sqrt{g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu}\).

title: Motion in flat spacetime
body: In an inertial Cartesian chart, \(ds^2=c^2dt^2-d\mathbf x^2\). Therefore \[d\tau\overset{\text{Minkowski metric}}{=}dt\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}.\] The annotation identifies the chosen metric, not an approximation. For \(v\ll c\), expansion gives \(d\tau\simeq dt(1-v^2/(2c^2))\). This distinguishes an exact clock relation from its slow-motion limit.
statement: The curved-spacetime clock integral recovers \(d\tau=dt\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\) in an inertial flat chart.

title: A clock held at fixed position
body: For a static diagonal metric with time coordinate \(ct\), a stationary clock has \(d\tau\overset{\text{fixed position}}{=}\sqrt{g_{00}}\,dt\). Different positions can have different rates relative to the same static time coordinate. Comparing those clocks requires a specified signal or meeting protocol; it is not a comparison of arbitrary coordinate labels.
statement: A clock fixed in a static chart ticks at \(d\tau=\sqrt{g_{00}}\,dt\), using \(x^0=ct\).

title: Null paths carry no clock frame
body: The timelike clock integral approaches zero along null displacement, but a photon has no rest frame or ticking proper-time clock. Use an affine parameter for null geodesics. Timelike free-fall paths locally extremise proper time; they are not universally the globally longest paths between arbitrary events.
statement: Null paths cannot carry a rest-frame clock; timelike proper-time extrema are local statements.

title: A nonzero direction with zero norm
body: A null curve has a nonzero tangent on the light cone at every point. Zero interval does not mean zero displacement. The Lorentzian signature allows cancellation between temporal and spatial contributions.
statement: A null tangent has zero metric norm without being the zero vector.

title: The null condition
body:
For a regular curve define \(k^\mu\coloneqq dx^\mu/d\lambda\). It is null when \[g_{\mu
u}k^\mu k^
u\overset{	ext{null condition}}{=}0,\qquad k^\mu
e0.\] Rescaling a monotonic parameter rescales the tangent but preserves its zero norm. This condition classifies the tangent; it does not specify how its direction evolves.
statement: A regular curve is null when its nonzero tangent satisfies \(g_{\mu\nu}k^\mu k^\nu=0\).

title: Light in a local frame
body: In a local inertial frame the condition is \(c^2dt^2-d\mathbf x^2=0\), hence lightlike motion has local speed \(c\). In general coordinates the corresponding coordinate speed may vary. At each event the metric, not a fixed drawing angle on the page, defines the light cone.
statement: The null condition gives local light speed \(c\), even when coordinate speeds differ.

title: Null does not automatically mean geodesic
body:
In geometric optics, freely propagating light in vacuum follows null geodesics. A prescribed null curve need not satisfy the geodesic equation. Bending or reflection by matter changes the physical situation, and finite-wavelength effects lie outside the ideal ray approximation. The geodesic law supplies information beyond the null constraint.

\explanation{constraint-versus-motion}{Why are two conditions needed?}{In a local inertial frame, setting the tangent norm to zero fixes the magnitude of the spatial velocity to \(c\). It does not prevent the direction from changing along a prescribed curve. The geodesic equation supplies the additional rule for an unforced ray; reflection or guiding by matter is a different situation.}
statement: The null constraint fixes the tangent’s causal type; the geodesic equation additionally governs its evolution.

title: No photon proper-time parameter
body: A null path has vanishing proper-time increment, so proper time cannot parametrise it. An affine parameter gives a useful tangent and geodesic equation, with a constant rescaling freedom. See \cref{geodesics}{gr.geodesic} and \cref{causal structure}{gr.causal_structure} for dynamics and global influence respectively.
statement: Proper time vanishes along a null path, so a null geodesic needs another parameter.

title: Which events can communicate?
body: The metric supplies local light cones. Their arrangement across spacetime determines which events can be connected by future-directed timelike or null curves. This global reachability is causal structure; no single coordinate separation reliably determines it in a general curved spacetime.
statement: Causal structure describes which events can be joined by future-directed causal paths.

title: Local directions and global reachability
body: After choosing a consistent time orientation, a future-directed timelike curve can represent a massive observer and a future-directed causal curve may also include null segments. The chronological future of an event uses timelike curves; its causal future allows both timelike and null curves. These are existence statements about entire paths.
statement: Timelike paths define chronological reachability; timelike or null paths define causal reachability.

title: Build influence from local cones
body:
At every point along a signal path the tangent must lie inside or on the future cone. A sequence of locally permitted directions may still fail to connect a chosen source to a distant receiver. Horizons arise from this global restriction, not from a local speed limit changing near the horizon.

The \cref{line element}{gr.line_element.definition} first classifies the allowed tangent directions; \cref{null curves}{gr.null_curve.definition} identify the boundary directions. A continuous path must obey this restriction at every event, not merely point toward the destination at its starting event. This is why local cone information must be assembled along an entire route before deciding whether communication is possible.
statement: Global causal reachability is built by following paths whose tangents stay within local future light cones.

title: Conformal rescaling
body: If \(\widetilde g_{\mu\nu}\coloneqq\Omega^2g_{\mu\nu}\) with smooth \(\Omega>0\), tangent norms gain a positive factor. Their signs and null directions stay the same, so causal curves are preserved. Clock times and lengths generally change. Causal structure therefore contains less information than the full metric.
statement: A smooth positive conformal rescaling preserves causal paths but generally changes clock times and lengths.

title: Cones do not guarantee good global causality
body: A Lorentzian metric alone does not rule out closed timelike curves or guarantee a global time function. Those are additional global properties. Likewise the coordinate tilt of a cone can change with the chart while physical reachability remains unchanged. Keep this distinction when studying an \cref{event horizon}{gr.event_horizon}.
statement: Local Lorentzian cones do not rule out global causal pathologies such as closed timelike curves.

title: Flat to first order
body: A smooth Lorentzian metric looks Minkowskian to first order in suitable coordinates around any regular event. This is a local approximation and an exact statement about values and first derivatives at a point, not a claim that curvature vanishes.
statement: At a regular event the metric can be Minkowskian through first order, while curvature remains.

title: Normal-coordinate conditions
body:
At a regular event \(p\), choose normal coordinates with origin \(x=0\). They give
\[ egin{aligned}g_{\mu
u}(p)&=\eta_{\mu
u},\ \partial_ho g_{\mu
u}(p)&=0.\end{aligned}\]
Thus nearby \(g_{\mu
u}(x)=\eta_{\mu
u}+O(x^2)\). The constant part is exactly Minkowskian and the linear correction vanishes. The order symbol retains the quadratic corrections; it does not set them to zero. These remaining changes can carry curvature.
statement: Normal coordinates give \(g(p)=\eta\), \(\partial g(p)=0\), and nearby corrections beginning at quadratic order.

title: Where curvature hides
body:
The Riemann tensor contains second metric derivatives as well as products of first derivatives. In normal coordinates the latter vanish at the origin while the former need not. Thus a local inertial laboratory can recover SR at the event and still detect tides by comparing separated trajectories.

\explanation{two-derivatives}{Why does removing first derivatives not remove curvature?}{A function can have zero slope at a point without being constant nearby: \(f(x)=1+ax^2\) is a simple example. Normal coordinates remove the metric's slope at their origin. Its quadratic changes remain, and suitable combinations of these second derivatives measure curvature. The analogy concerns the Taylor expansion, not a claim that one scalar function describes the full geometry.}
statement: Second metric derivatives can encode tides even when first derivatives vanish at the chosen event.

title: A scale for the approximation
body: If typical curvature components have magnitude of order \(1/L^2\), a laboratory of extent \(\ell\) has metric corrections of order \((\ell/L)^2\) in normal coordinates. This is a scale estimate, not a universal bound. Large boosts or rapidly varying curvature can change which components and duration matter for an actual experiment.
statement: Typical curvature scale \(L\) gives normal-coordinate metric corrections of order \((\ell/L)^2\) over size \(\ell\).

title: Pointwise flattening is not a field equation
body: Local flatness is available for any sufficiently smooth nondegenerate Lorentzian metric, regardless of whether it solves Einstein's equations. The physical equivalence principle additionally says that local nongravitational laws use this metric. Singular boundaries are outside the regular-point assumptions.
statement: Local flatness is a regular-metric property, not a consequence of Einstein’s field equations.

title: Fix signs before using formulas
body: Lorentzian geometry distinguishes one temporal direction from three spatial directions. Either overall sign convention describes the same causal physics when every dependent definition is translated consistently. This atlas uses \(+---\) in both SR and GR.
statement: This atlas uses \(+---\); changing convention preserves physics only when associated formulas are translated.

title: The atlas convention
body: In an orthonormal frame set \[\eta_{\mu\nu}\coloneqq\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1).\] For a nonzero vector, positive norm is timelike, zero norm null and negative norm spacelike. The signature counts positive and negative directions of the quadratic form; it is not the signs of arbitrary diagonal entries in a chart with cross terms.
statement: With \(+---\), positive norm is timelike, negative norm spacelike, and a nonzero zero-norm vector is null.

title: Time and units
body: Use \(x^0\coloneqq ct\) when retaining SI dimensions, and announce \(c\overset{\text{units}}{=}1\) when switching to natural units. Then a proper-time tangent obeys \(g_{\mu\nu}u^\mu u^\nu\overset{\text{proper-time normalisation}}{=}c^2\), or one in natural units. The numerical convention does not change the physical speed of light.
statement: Using \(x^0=ct\) gives \(g(u,u)=c^2\); in announced natural units this becomes one.

title: Translate a source carefully
body: Tong uses \(-+++\), whereas these concepts use \(+---\). Multiplying the metric by minus one changes scalar contractions and stress-energy formulas expressed with the metric. A perfect fluid consequently has a minus pressure term in the atlas convention. Connection coefficients are unchanged by a constant overall metric sign flip.
statement: An overall metric sign reversal leaves the Levi-Civita connection unchanged but changes contractions.

title: Signature does not fix curvature sign
body: Authors also choose an independent sign and index convention for the Riemann tensor. That choice propagates to Ricci curvature, the Einstein equations and the action. Check the full convention bundle in the notation glossary, not just the signature, before importing a formula. No physical conclusion should depend on mixing conventions from two sources.
statement: Metric signature and Riemann sign are independent conventions that must be checked together.

title: Compare fields at neighbouring events
body:
A vector at one event belongs to that event's tangent space. A vector at the next event belongs to a different tangent space. Before asking whether a vector field has changed, we therefore need a rule for comparing these spaces.

Coordinates alone are not enough. They label components, but their basis vectors may turn or change scale from place to place. So a component derivative can mix a genuine field change with a change in the measuring basis.

A connection supplies the comparison rule. Its covariant derivative separates those effects, and its transport equation carries a vector along a chosen path. These two uses describe the same additional geometric structure.

\explanation{polar-arrow}{Why can a constant arrow have changing components?}{In a flat plane, an arrow that always points east has different radial and angular components at different locations, because the polar basis turns with position. The connection accounts for that turning. This happens even though the plane has no curvature.}
statement: A connection supplies the extra rule needed to compare vectors in neighbouring tangent spaces.

title: A derivative with a direction
body:
Write \(
abla_XV\) for the covariant derivative of a vector field \(V\) in direction \(X\). It is linear in the direction and obeys the product rule \[
abla_X(fV)=X(f)V+f
abla_XV.\] The term \(X(f)\) differentiates the scalar coefficient, while the other term differentiates the vector field itself. These properties let a local rule extend consistently to tensor fields.
statement: A connection differentiates vector fields along directions and obeys linearity and the product rule.

title: Connection coefficients
body:
In a coordinate basis define \(
abla_{\partial_\mu}\partial_
u\coloneqq\Gamma^ho{}_{\mu
u}\partial_ho\). The coefficients describe the change of the basis under the chosen comparison rule. They are not tensor components: coordinate changes add a term involving second coordinate derivatives.
statement: Connection coefficients specify how the chosen comparison rule differentiates a coordinate basis.

title: The standard GR choice
body:
A connection can exist without a metric. Standard GR uses the unique torsion-free connection compatible with the metric, called the Levi-Civita connection. Thus the metric supplies both measurements and the comparison rule. Metric compatibility alone would not select a unique connection if torsion were allowed.

The metric fixes lengths and inner products; compatibility asks transport to preserve them. Torsion-freedom imposes an independent symmetry condition. Taken together, these conditions determine the Levi-Civita comparison rule. Neither condition alone is the definition of a general connection.
statement: Standard GR selects the unique metric-compatible, torsion-free connection.

title: Connection is not curvature
body: Nonzero coefficients can occur in flat spacetime, for example in polar coordinates. Curvature concerns the failure of transport to agree around infinitesimal loops and is tensorial. A local inertial chart can remove coefficients at an event without removing curvature. See \cref{Christoffel symbols}{gr.christoffel_symbols} for computation and \cref{parallel transport}{gr.parallel_transport} for the pathwise interpretation.
statement: Nonzero connection coefficients can reflect a changing basis in flat spacetime.

title: Compute the metric's connection
body: Christoffel symbols turn a metric into a practical differentiation and free-fall rule. Their numerical values depend on the coordinate basis; the geometric connection they represent does not depend on a particular chart.
statement: The Levi-Civita coefficients express the metric’s comparison rule in a coordinate basis.

title: The Levi-Civita formula
body:
For the metric-compatible, torsion-free connection define the derivative combination
\[ egin{aligned}C_{\sigma\mu
u}&\coloneqq\partial_\mu g_{\sigma
u}+\partial_
u g_{\sigma\mu}\ &\quad-\partial_\sigma g_{\mu
u}.\end{aligned}\]
The Christoffel symbols are then
\[\Gamma^ho{}_{\mu
u}=	frac12g^{ho\sigma}C_{\sigma\mu
u}.\]
This is the Levi-Civita formula. The inverse metric raises the remaining index. A general connection need not have this form; both compatibility and torsion-freedom are essential assumptions.
statement: Metric compatibility and zero torsion uniquely fix the Levi-Civita coefficients.

title: Where the formula comes from
body:
Given \cref{metric compatibility}{gr.metric_compatibility.definition}, expand three equations obtained by permuting the indices. Write a lowered coefficient as \(\Gamma_{a b c}\coloneqq g_{aho}\Gamma^ho{}_{bc}\). Then
\[ egin{aligned}\partial_\mu g_{
u\sigma}&=\Gamma_{\sigma\mu
u}+\Gamma_{
u\mu\sigma},\ \partial_
u g_{\mu\sigma}&=\Gamma_{\sigma
u\mu}+\Gamma_{\mu
u\sigma},\ \partial_\sigma g_{\mu
u}&=\Gamma_{
u\sigma\mu}+\Gamma_{\mu\sigma
u}.\end{aligned}\]
Now add the first two and subtract the third. \cref{Zero torsion}{gr.torsion_free_connection.definition} makes the last two indices of each lowered coefficient symmetric, so the unwanted pairs cancel. The result is
\[ egin{aligned}2\Gamma_{\sigma\mu
u}&=\partial_\mu g_{
u\sigma}+\partial_
u g_{\mu\sigma}\ &\quad-\partial_\sigma g_{\mu
u}.\end{aligned}\]
Multiplying by \(g^{ho\sigma}/2\) gives the Levi-Civita formula. This explicitly combines a measurement-preserving comparison rule, a symmetry condition and the inverse metric.
statement: Combining three metric-compatibility equations cancels unwanted coefficients and isolates the connection.

title: Flat space in polar coordinates
body:
For the spatial plane with metric \(d\ell^2=dr^2+r^2d\phi^2\), the nonzero coefficients include \(\Gamma^r{}_{\phi\phi}=-r\) and \(\Gamma^\phi{}_{r\phi}=1/r\). They account for changing radial and angular basis vectors even though the plane is flat. The same coefficients occur for the corresponding negative spatial sector of a flat Lorentzian metric.

\explanation{polar-calculation}{Calculate the radial coefficient}{Only \(g_{\phi\phi}=r^2\) varies, so \(\partial_r g_{\phi\phi}=2r\). For \(\Gamma^r{}_{\phi\phi}\), the two angular derivatives vanish and the remaining term is \(-\tfrac12 g^{rr}\partial_r g_{\phi\phi}=-r\). The correction records basis changes, not a gravitational force.}
statement: Polar-coordinate Christoffel symbols are nonzero even on a flat plane.

title: Do not test curvature by inspection
body: A coefficient that vanishes in one chart can be nonzero in another. A genuine tensor that vanishes at an event vanishes there in every nonsingular chart. Build the Riemann tensor before concluding that gravity is intrinsic. For calculations, first invert the metric, then take derivatives, and use lower-index symmetry to reduce repeated work.
statement: Curvature is tensorial; the vanishing or nonvanishing of a Christoffel symbol is chart-dependent.

title: Differentiate the field, not just its components
body:
Suppose we differentiate \(V=V^\nu\partial_\nu\) along a coordinate direction. The product rule differentiates both the component \(V^\nu\) and the basis vector \(\partial_\nu\). The ordinary derivative of the components includes only the first contribution.

The \cref{connection}{gr.connection.authored_3} tells us how to supply the second contribution. Combining them gives a tensorial derivative, so observers using different coordinate grids agree about the geometric change even though their component calculations differ.

This is the reason for the connection correction. It is not a prescription to add an arbitrary force to every derivative.
statement: Covariant differentiation corrects component changes for the changing coordinate basis.

title: Vectors and covectors
body:
For a vector \(V\) and a covector \(w\), the coordinate formulas are
\[ egin{aligned}
abla_\mu V^
u&\coloneqq\partial_\mu V^
u+\Gamma^
u{}_{\muho}V^ho,\ 
abla_\mu w_
u&\coloneqq\partial_\mu w_
u-\Gamma^ho{}_{\mu
u}w_ho.\end{aligned}\]
There is one correction for each index of a general tensor. A scalar has no indices to correct, so its first covariant derivative is just its ordinary gradient. The rules preserve contractions as well as the product rule.
statement: Each upper tensor index contributes a plus connection correction and each lower index a minus correction.

title: Why the covector sign differs
body:
The contraction \(w_
u V^
u\) is a scalar. Requiring the product rule and \(
abla_\mu(w_
u V^
u)=\partial_\mu(w_
u V^
u)\) makes the two connection corrections cancel. The minus sign is therefore required for differentiation to commute with contraction, not an arbitrary sign convention for covectors.

\explanation{sign-cancellation}{Check the cancellation explicitly}{Insert both derivative rules into \((
abla_\mu w_
u)V^
u+w_
u
abla_\mu V^
u\). The extra terms are \(-\Gamma^ho{}_{\mu
u}w_ho V^
u\) and \(w_
u\Gamma^
u{}_{\muho}V^ho\). Exchanging the dummy labels \(ho\) and \(
u\) in the second term shows that they cancel, leaving the ordinary derivative of the scalar contraction.}
statement: The covector correction must cancel the vector correction when their contraction is differentiated.

title: A scalar's second derivative
body:
A scalar satisfies \(
abla_\mu f=\partial_\mu f\), but its gradient is a covector. Hence \[
abla_\mu
abla_
u f=\partial_\mu\partial_
u f-\Gamma^ho{}_{\mu
u}\partial_ho f.\] Omitting the connection in the second derivative would generally destroy tensorial transformation. For a torsion-free connection the two derivative indices commute on a scalar.
statement: A scalar’s first derivative is ordinary, but its second derivative must treat the gradient as a covector.

title: Covariant is not constant
body:
A field with constant coordinate components need not have zero covariant derivative. Conversely a parallel field may have changing components. Along a curve with tangent \(u\), the directional derivative is \(D V^\mu/D\lambda\coloneqq u^
u
abla_
u V^\mu\). This is the derivative in \cref{parallel transport}{gr.parallel_transport}.
statement: Constant components need not mean covariant constancy, because the basis can change.

title: Transport preserves measurement
body: A metric measures inner products at each point. Compatibility asks that the connection's transport respect those measurements, so a vector carried parallel along a path does not change its norm merely because it reaches another tangent space.
statement: Metric compatibility makes the connection’s comparison rule preserve inner products.

title: The compatibility condition
body:
A metric-compatible connection satisfies \[
abla_ho g_{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{compatibility}}{=}0.\] In components this is \(\partial_ho g_{\mu
u}=\Gamma^\sigma{}_{ho\mu}g_{\sigma
u}+\Gamma^\sigma{}_{ho
u}g_{\mu\sigma}\). Ordinary metric derivatives need not vanish; connection terms balance them.
statement: A metric-compatible connection satisfies \(\nabla_\rho g_{\mu\nu}=0\).

title: Preservation along a curve
body:
Let \(V\) and \(W\) be parallel along a curve with tangent \(u\). The product rule gives three possible contributions to the change in their scalar product:
\[\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{d\lambda}g(V,W)&=(\nabla_u g)(V,W)\\ &\quad+g(\nabla_uV,W)\\ &\quad+g(V,\nabla_uW).\end{aligned}\]
Metric compatibility sets the first term to zero. Parallel transport sets the other two to zero. So \(g(V,W)\) stays constant along the path.

Both inputs matter: compatibility says the comparison rule respects the metric, while parallel transport says these particular vectors are being carried by that rule. A vector that an instrument actively rotates need not satisfy the second condition.
statement: Compatibility and parallel transport together keep the scalar product of transported vectors fixed.

title: Index movement commutes with differentiation
statement: Compatibility allows indices to be raised or lowered before or after covariant differentiation.

title: Norm preservation does not imply no curvature
body: A vector may return rotated after transport around a loop while keeping its norm. Compatibility preserves metric comparisons, not path independence. Compatibility also does not force torsion to vanish; imposing both conditions selects the \cref{Levi-Civita connection}{gr.christoffel_symbols}.
statement: Preserving norms permits path-dependent rotation and does not by itself remove torsion.

title: A second condition on transport
body: Standard GR uses both metric compatibility and zero torsion. These are independent conditions. Torsion describes an antisymmetric part of the comparison rule; curvature describes how transport around a loop changes a vector.
statement: Zero torsion and metric compatibility are independent conditions; standard GR imposes both.

title: A tensor built from the connection
body:
To avoid confusing torsion with stress-energy, write \[\mathcal T(X,Y)\coloneqq
abla_XY-
abla_YX-[X,Y].\] In a coordinate basis, where the basis commutators vanish, \(\mathcal T^ho{}_{\mu
u}=\Gamma^ho{}_{\mu
u}-\Gamma^ho{}_{
u\mu}\). Zero torsion therefore makes the lower coefficient indices symmetric in that basis.
statement: Torsion subtracts the vector-field commutator from the antisymmetrised covariant derivative.

title: Why the basis qualification matters
body:
In a noncoordinate frame the basis vectors need not commute. Their commutator contributes to the torsion formula, so simply antisymmetrising coefficients is insufficient. Torsion itself is a tensor even though the coefficients used to calculate it are not.

\explanation{commuting-basis}{What is special about coordinate directions?}{Coordinate directions correspond to changing independent labels. For smooth functions their mixed partial derivatives commute, so \([\partial_\mu,\partial_\nu]=0\). A freely chosen frame, such as locally normalised directions that vary across space, need not have this property. The commutator term removes that frame effect from the definition of torsion.}
statement: Symmetric lower coefficients characterise zero torsion only in a coordinate basis.

title: A scalar commutator
body:
For a scalar \(f\), the difference of its second covariant derivatives is \((
abla_\mu
abla_
u-
abla_
u
abla_\mu)f=-\mathcal T^ho{}_{\mu
u}\partial_ho f\) in a coordinate basis. It vanishes for the standard torsion-free connection. Vectors can still have a nonzero derivative commutator because curvature acts on their indices.
statement: The antisymmetric second covariant derivative of a scalar measures torsion in a coordinate basis.

title: Zero torsion does not mean flat spacetime
body: Schwarzschild spacetime uses a torsion-free connection and has nonzero curvature. The two conditions measure different failures of Euclidean intuition. The schematic infinitesimal parallelogram picture refers to the leading closure defect, not a guarantee that every finite loop behaves as in flat space.
statement: Torsion-free curved geometries are common; zero torsion does not imply zero curvature.

title: Carry a vector along a specified path
body:
The phrase “keep the arrow pointing the same way” is clear in a flat Cartesian plane. On a curved surface, or in a varying coordinate basis, it needs a comparison rule.

A \cref{connection}{gr.connection} supplies that rule. Along a chosen parametrised curve, require the covariant change of the vector to vanish. The resulting differential equation determines the carried vector from its initial value.

The route is essential data. Two routes can produce different final arrows even when they start and end at the same events. Parallel transport therefore compares tangent spaces along a path, rather than identifying all tangent spaces once and for all.
statement: A connection, a path and an initial vector determine a parallel-transported vector along that path.

title: The transport equation
body: For a curve \(x^\mu(\lambda)\) and vector \(V^\mu(\lambda)\), parallel transport means \[\frac{DV^\mu}{D\lambda}\coloneqq\frac{dV^\mu}{d\lambda}+\Gamma^\mu{}_{\alpha\beta}\frac{dx^\alpha}{d\lambda}V^\beta\overset{\text{parallel}}{=}0.\] The connection correction distinguishes constant geometric direction from constant coordinate components.
statement: A parallel vector satisfies \(DV^\mu/D\lambda=0\) along the specified curve.

title: Moving round a sphere
body:
On a sphere, carry a tangent arrow along a geodesic triangle. It can return to its starting point with a different orientation. Each segment was parallel transport; the discrepancy reflects curvature integrated over the loop. This positive-definite example illustrates the comparison rule, while spacetime uses a Lorentzian metric and can mix temporal and spatial directions.

For a concrete route on a unit sphere, travel from the equator to the north pole along a meridian, back down a meridian a quarter-turn away, and return along the equator. Each leg is a geodesic. A parallel arrow turns by a net right angle on returning, even though no local instruction ever told it to rotate within the tangent plane. The accumulated discrepancy reflects the enclosed spherical area.
statement: Transport around a geodesic triangle on a sphere can return an arrow rotated.

title: Preserved norm, path-dependent result
body: The Levi-Civita connection preserves inner products of parallel vectors, so timelike, spacelike and null character are preserved. Different routes between the same endpoints can nevertheless yield different final vectors. Curvature controls this effect for infinitesimal loops; topology can also matter for transport around noncontractible loops.
statement: Metric-compatible transport preserves scalar products but need not be independent of route.

title: Transport is not the motion law for every object
body: A vector carried by a rotating or accelerating instrument need not be parallel transported. A geodesic is the special case where the curve's own tangent is parallel along itself. Specify both the transported object and the path before interpreting a change in components or a loop comparison.
statement: An instrument’s carried vector is parallel only if its acceleration and rotation obey the transport rule.

title: Straightest motion in curved spacetime
body: A geodesic is defined by its tangent's transport, not by how straight a curve looks on a coordinate plot. With the Levi-Civita connection, timelike geodesics describe ideal freely falling massive bodies and null geodesics describe vacuum light rays in geometric optics.
statement: A geodesic carries its own tangent parallel along itself; its coordinate picture need not be straight.

title: An affine tangent
body: For \(v^\mu\coloneqq dx^\mu/d\lambda\), the affine geodesic condition is \[\nabla_vv\overset{\text{geodesic}}{=}0.\] The parameter \(\lambda\) is affine; another parameter of the form \(a\lambda+b\), with constant nonzero \(a\), is affine too. A general reparameterisation leaves the curve but adds a tangent-proportional term to its equation.
statement: For an affine parameter, a geodesic obeys \(\nabla_vv=0\).

title: Choose the causal type initially
body:
Metric compatibility gives \(d[g(v,v)]/d\lambda\overset{\text{geodesic}}{=}0\). Thus the initial tangent determines whether the path remains timelike, null or spacelike. Proper time is an affine parameter for a timelike geodesic. Null curves have no nonzero proper-time increment and need a different affine parameter.

The combination is direct: metric compatibility lets us differentiate the scalar product, and the geodesic law removes both tangent derivatives:
\[\frac{d}{d\lambda}g(v,v)=2g(\nabla_vv,v)=0.\]
So a tangent initially inside the light cone stays timelike; one on its boundary stays null. This does not require constant coordinate components.
statement: A Levi-Civita geodesic preserves its tangent norm and therefore its initial causal type.

title: Local straightness and global shape
body: In local inertial coordinates, an affine geodesic has zero coordinate acceleration at the chosen event. Elsewhere its plotted path may bend because the connection coefficients change. In a sufficiently small normal neighbourhood the initial position and tangent determine a unique geodesic, but global connecting geodesics can be multiple or absent.
statement: Local straightness fixes a geodesic from initial data, without guaranteeing a unique global route between endpoints.

title: Stationary is not globally shortest
body: For timelike paths the variational statement concerns stationary proper time, locally maximal for short enough segments without conjugate points. It is not a universal shortest-distance rule. Spacelike geodesics are useful geometric curves, not possible histories of massive observers.
statement: Short timelike geodesics locally maximise proper time; there is no universal global shortest-path rule.

title: A differential equation for free paths
body: The coordinate form of geodesic motion balances ordinary coordinate acceleration against connection terms. Given a smooth metric, initial event and tangent, it is a second-order system for the path.
statement: The coordinate geodesic equation balances component acceleration with basis-change terms.

title: Affine parameter form
body: Expanding \(\nabla_vv=0\) yields \[\frac{d^2x^\mu}{d\lambda^2}+\Gamma^\mu{}_{\alpha\beta}\frac{dx^\alpha}{d\lambda}\frac{dx^\beta}{d\lambda}\overset{\text{affine geodesic}}{=}0.\] The annotation states the motion law and parameter assumption. The Christoffel contribution is not a nongravitational force measured by an accelerometer.
statement: An affine geodesic satisfies \(\ddot x^\mu+\Gamma^\mu{}_{\alpha\beta}\dot x^\alpha\dot x^\beta=0\).

title: A straight line in polar coordinates
body: In a flat spatial plane the radial and angular equations are \(\ddot r-r\dot\phi^2=0\) and \(\ddot\phi+2\dot r\dot\phi/r=0\). Dots denote an affine parameter. These apparently accelerated coordinate motions describe Cartesian straight lines. They provide a useful check before interpreting a nonzero connection term as curvature.
statement: Polar-coordinate geodesic equations can describe ordinary straight lines in a flat plane.

title: Check normalisation and parameter
body:
For a timelike path with proper time, impose \(g_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu=c^2\); for a null affine tangent impose zero norm. These constraints are preserved by exact geodesic evolution and are useful checks on a calculation. With arbitrary parameter \(s\), the right-hand side becomes \(f(s)dx^\mu/ds\), which changes the parameter rather than the unparameterised path.

\explanation{parameter-term}{Where does the extra parameter term come from?}{Let \(\lambda\) be affine and write \(q=d\lambda/ds\). The new tangent is \(dx/ds=qv\). Differentiating covariantly gives \(D(qv)/Ds=(dq/ds)v\), since \(Dv/D\lambda=0\). Thus the right-hand side is \((d\ln|q|/ds)dx/ds\). It lies along the tangent and changes the speed of tracing the curve, not the curve itself.}
statement: Geodesic evolution preserves tangent norm; a nonaffine parameter adds a tangent-proportional term.

title: Coordinate time is usually not affine
body: Replacing proper time by a convenient coordinate time without the extra term changes the equation. Also keep the test-body assumptions: contact forces, thrust and finite-size effects require additional dynamics. See \cref{four-acceleration}{gr.four_acceleration} for the covariant force measure.
statement: Using coordinate time as if it were affine generally omits a necessary term.

title: Free fall from stationary clock time
body: The massive-particle action weights the proper length of a timelike path. Holding the metric and endpoint events fixed, varying the intervening path gives the geodesic equation. This connects geometric free fall to the earlier action principle.
statement: Stationary proper time supplies a variational description of massive free-fall paths.

title: The invariant path action
body:
For a massive test particle with a timelike path and fixed endpoints, define
\[S\coloneqq-mc^2\int d\tau.\]
Using a parameter \(\lambda\), write \(Q\coloneqq g_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu>0\). The same action is \(S=-mc\int\sqrt Q\,d\lambda\), because the proper-time definition gives \(d\tau=\sqrt Q\,d\lambda/c\).

The square root makes this functional independent of an increasing relabelling of the path parameter. Requiring \(\delta S=0\) for fixed-endpoint path variations selects timelike geodesics; the metric is held fixed during the variation.
statement: The massive particle action \(S=-mc^2\int d\tau\) is invariant under monotonic path relabelling.

title: A convenient quadratic calculation
body:
For a fixed metric, vary paths with fixed endpoints in
\[S_q=\int	frac12g_{\mu
u}\dot x^\mu\dot x^
u\,d\lambda.\]
The parameter is not fixed by a square root here: the resulting equation selects affine parametrisation. With \(L=	frac12g_{\mu
u}\dot x^\mu\dot x^
u\), its two derivatives are
\[ egin{aligned} rac{\partial L}{\partial\dot x^ho}&=g_{ho
u}\dot x^
u,\  rac{\partial L}{\partial x^ho}&=	frac12\partial_ho g_{\mu
u}\dot x^\mu\dot x^
u.\end{aligned}\]
The Euler–Lagrange equation therefore becomes
\[ egin{aligned}0&=g_{ho
u}\ddot x^
u\ &\quad+\partial_\mu g_{ho
u}\dot x^\mu\dot x^
u\ &\quad-	frac12\partial_ho g_{\mu
u}\dot x^\mu\dot x^
u.\end{aligned}\]
The symmetric velocity product lets us symmetrise the middle term. Multiplying by the inverse metric then groups the derivatives into the \cref{Levi-Civita combination}{gr.christoffel_symbols.definition}, giving \(\ddot x^\sigma+\Gamma^\sigma{}_{\mu
u}\dot x^\mu\dot x^
u=0\).

\explanation{square-root-affine}{Why may the quadratic calculation replace the massive square root?}{Vary the square-root action first, and only then choose a parameter for which \(g(\dot x,\dot x)\) is constant and positive. Its equation reduces to the same affine geodesic equation. Setting the norm constant before varying the square-root integrand would instead throw away the path dependence that produces the equation.}
statement: Varying the quadratic metric action gives the affine geodesic equation.

title: Do not vary a zero null length
body: The massive square-root action cannot simply be restricted to null curves before variation: it then supplies no useful path functional. The quadratic action with an initially null tangent yields affine null geodesics, or an auxiliary-variable action can enforce the null constraint. Distinguish this from assigning a proper-time clock to light.
statement: The massive square-root action must not be set to zero on null curves before variation.

title: What is varied
body: The path, not the spacetime metric, is varied here. Metric variation belongs to the Einstein-Hilbert action. Stationary proper time also does not promise a global maximum for long paths; local extrema and conjugate points matter.
statement: Particle variation changes a path in a fixed metric; gravitational variation changes the metric itself.

title: A local tangent normalised by a clock
body: Four-velocity describes a massive observer's motion as a vector in the tangent space at each event. Its normalisation follows from proper time, so it is more constrained than the tangent formed with an arbitrary curve parameter.
statement: Four-velocity is the timelike tangent scaled by the observer’s own clock.

title: Definition and normalisation
body: Define \(u^\mu\coloneqq dx^\mu/d\tau\). With signature \(+---\), \[g_{\mu\nu}u^\mu u^\nu\overset{\text{proper time}}{=}c^2.\] Natural units set the right-hand side to one. The constant norm does not require constant components; the observer may accelerate or move through a varying metric.
statement: Proper-time parametrisation fixes \(u^\mu=dx^\mu/d\tau\) and \(g(u,u)=c^2\).

title: An instantaneous local measurement
body: In an orthonormal frame, \(u^{\hat a}=\gamma(c,\mathbf v)\) with \(\gamma\coloneqq(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}\). Hatted indices denote frame components. This familiar SR expression applies locally; replacing frame components by arbitrary coordinate components can give incorrect measured speeds.
statement: The familiar SR expression \(u^{\hat a}=\gamma(c,\mathbf v)\) uses local orthonormal, not arbitrary coordinate, components.

title: Compare observers at one event
body:
Two future-directed unit clock tangents \(u,w\) meeting at an event have relative Lorentz factor \(\gamma_{\mathrm{rel}}\coloneqq g(u,w)/c^2\). It equals one for comoving observers and exceeds one for relative motion. Comparing velocities at separated events additionally requires a transport or observation prescription.

\explanation{relative-gamma}{Recover the familiar Lorentz factor}{Use the instantaneous orthonormal rest frame of the first observer, so \(u^{\hat a}=(c,0,0,0)\). The second has \(w^{\hat a}=\gamma(c,\mathbf v)\). With signature \(+---\), their product is \(g(u,w)=\gamma c^2\). Since this scalar product is coordinate-independent, the result can then be used in any chart at the meeting event.}
statement: At one event, the metric contraction of two clock tangents gives their relative Lorentz factor.

title: No massive four-velocity for light
body: A photon has a null tangent or four-momentum, not a four-velocity parametrised by proper time. The distinction prevents dividing by a vanishing proper-time increment. The GR concept keeps the local SR interpretation while making tangent-space location explicit.
statement: A null particle has no proper-time four-velocity; use a null tangent or four-momentum.

title: Acceleration that an instrument measures
body: Four-acceleration measures how a massive observer departs from geodesic motion. Unlike a second coordinate derivative, it is a vector. Its magnitude is the proper acceleration registered by an ideal accelerometer.
statement: Four-acceleration measures departure from geodesic motion and gives an accelerometer’s proper acceleration.

title: Covariant change of velocity
body: Define \[a^\mu\coloneqq\frac{Du^\mu}{D\tau}=\frac{du^\mu}{d\tau}+\Gamma^\mu{}_{\alpha\beta}u^\alpha u^\beta.\] Free fall imposes \(a^\mu\overset{\text{geodesic}}{=}0\). In the atlas convention define the measured magnitude by \(\alpha\coloneqq\sqrt{-g_{\mu\nu}a^\mu a^\nu}\).
statement: The proper-time covariant derivative of four-velocity defines \(a^\mu\); its magnitude is \(\sqrt{-g(a,a)}\).

title: Orthogonality to velocity
body:
Differentiate the normalisation \(g(u,u)=c^2\). Metric compatibility and the product rule give \[0\overset{\text{fixed norm}}{=}\frac{d}{d\tau}g(u,u)=2g(u,a).\] Thus acceleration is orthogonal to the timelike velocity and is spacelike unless zero. In the instantaneous rest frame its time component vanishes.

\explanation{spacelike-acceleration}{Why must nonzero acceleration be spacelike?}{In the observer's instantaneous rest frame, \(u=(c,\mathbf0)\). Orthogonality then requires \(a^{\hat0}=0\), leaving only spatial components. With \(+---\), their norm is negative. The minus sign in \(\sqrt{-g(a,a)}\) therefore produces a real positive instrument reading.}
statement: Metric compatibility and fixed velocity norm imply \(g(u,a)=0\).

title: A supported observer
body: A rocket held at constant radius outside a spherical body has nonzero proper acceleration, although its radial coordinate is fixed. An orbiting test body can have zero proper acceleration despite a changing coordinate velocity. The distinction is between support or thrust and geometrically free motion, not between moving and stationary pictures.
statement: Hovering requires proper acceleration even at fixed coordinates; free orbit can have none.

title: Notation and scope
body: Use lowercase \(a^\mu\) here, reserving electromagnetic \(A^\mu\) for the potential. The magnitude is coordinate-independent, but its spatial direction is measured relative to a frame. Accelerating frames and finite-body tidal stresses need separate treatment; zero four-acceleration does not imply zero curvature.
statement: Zero four-acceleration says one observer is freely falling, not that neighbouring tidal effects vanish.

title: Measure curvature with a family of falls
body: Geodesic deviation compares nearby free-fall paths rather than one observer's coordinate acceleration. It makes tidal gravity quantitative. Work to first order in separation, with a smooth family of affinely parametrised geodesics.
statement: A smooth family of nearby geodesics makes tidal relative acceleration a first-order curvature measurement.

title: The separation equation
body: Let \(u\) be the geodesic tangent and \(\xi\) the connecting vector of a family whose parameter directions commute. With the glossary's Riemann convention, \[\frac{D^2\xi^\rho}{D\tau^2}\overset{\text{geodesic deviation}}{=}R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu}u^\sigma u^\mu\xi^\nu.\] A source with the opposite Riemann definition writes the opposite sign. The index order is part of the convention.
statement: For commuting family directions, curvature determines the second covariant derivative of the separation vector.

Let \(u\) run along each affinely parametrised geodesic and let \(\xi\) connect equal parameter values on neighbouring geodesics. For a smooth two-parameter family, \([u,\xi]=0\). Zero torsion then gives \(
abla_u\xi=
abla_\xi u\).

Using the atlas convention \(R(u,\xi)=[

Thus the \cref{tidal comparison}{gr.tidal_gravity.definition} is not a new force added to either geodesic. It follows from comparing two free trajectories using a torsion-free connection; curvature measures the obstruction to commuting those comparisons.

Differentiation with respect to \(	au\) gives \(u\), while differentiation with respect to the neighbouring-path label \(s\) gives \(\xi\). A small label difference times \(\xi\) approximates physical separation to first order. At finite separation the linear equation is no longer exact.}
statement: Commuting derivatives along neighbouring geodesics leaves the Riemann curvature term.

title: Recover Newtonian tides
body: For slowly moving neighbours in a weak static field, the spatial equation becomes \(d^2\xi^i/dt^2\simeq-\partial_i\partial_j\Phi\,\xi^j\). A point mass stretches radial separations and squeezes transverse ones. This limit checks the convention's physical sign against the earlier tidal-gravity example.
statement: The weak-field, slow-motion limit recovers the potential Hessian’s stretching and squeezing.

title: Relative motion needs initial data
body: Even in flat spacetime neighbouring geodesics can have nonzero initial relative velocity; their separation then changes linearly. Curvature determines covariant relative acceleration. For finite separations the linear deviation approximation fails, and non-geodesic observers introduce additional acceleration terms.
statement: Curvature governs relative acceleration, while initial separation and relative velocity remain independent data.

title: Curvature survives a change of coordinates
body: A connection compares vectors at neighbouring events. Curvature measures the local failure of those comparisons to agree around a loop. It controls tidal acceleration even in a freely falling frame where the connection coefficients vanish at one event.

title: Fix the derivative order
body:
For the Levi-Civita connection our convention is \[[
