title: From connection to tensor
What the indices measure
body: The indices \(\mu,\nu\) select the oriented plane of a small loop, \(\sigma\) the transported vector component and \(\rho\) the resulting change. With its first index lowered, Riemann is antisymmetric within each index pair, symmetric under exchange of pairs, and obeys a cyclic identity. These symmetries leave 20 independent components in four dimensions.

title: Zero coefficients are not zero curvature
body: In normal coordinates \(\Gamma(p)=0\), but its derivatives at \(p\) generally remain. Flatness requires Riemann to vanish throughout a neighbourhood, not merely a convenient choice of coefficients. The same tensor supplies the relative acceleration in \cref{geodesic deviation}{gr.geodesic_deviation}; contractions give the \cref{Ricci tensor}{gr.ricci_tensor}.

title: Trace the tidal map
body: Riemann describes directional tidal stretching and transport. Ricci is a contraction that retains the trace of this information. It is especially useful for the volume behaviour of nearby freely falling trajectories and for coupling geometry to matter.

title: Contract a specific pair
body: With the atlas curvature convention, define \[R_{\mu\nu}\coloneqq R^\rho{}_{\mu\rho\nu}.\] The summed index is the first upper and third lower slot of Riemann as written. For the Levi-Civita connection the result is symmetric, so it has ten independent components in four dimensions.

title: Volume change versus shape change
body:
An initially comoving small cloud can stretch in one direction while shrinking in another. The trace of its tidal acceleration involves \(R_{\mu
u}u^\mu u^
u\), while directional distortions require more of Riemann. For an initially nonexpanding, shear-free, rotation-free timelike geodesic bundle, the initial expansion rate obeys \(d	heta/d	au=-R_{\mu
u}u^\mu u^
u\). In general shear, rotation and existing expansion also contribute.

title: Vacuum can still produce tides
body: Outside an isolated spherical mass, with zero cosmological constant, \(R_{\mu\nu}\overset{\text{vacuum EFE}}{=}0\). Nevertheless a falling cloud stretches radially and contracts transversely. The remaining trace-free part of Riemann, called Weyl curvature, carries this tidal information. Ricci-flat therefore does not mean flat.

title: The next contraction
body: Contracting Ricci with the inverse metric gives the \cref{Ricci scalar}{gr.ricci_scalar}. Combining that scalar with Ricci gives the \cref{Einstein tensor}{gr.einstein_tensor}. Each contraction discards information; none is an interchangeable name for the full curvature tensor.

title: A scalar from curvature
body: The Ricci scalar assigns a coordinate-independent number to each event by tracing the Ricci tensor with the metric. It is compact enough to serve as a gravitational action integrand, but contains much less information than either Ricci or Riemann.

title: A metric trace
body: Define \[R\coloneqq g^{\mu\nu}R_{\mu\nu}.\] This is a tensor contraction, not the ordinary sum of diagonal entries in an arbitrary chart. In a local orthonormal frame of signature \(+---\), it reads \(R\overset{\text{orthonormal frame}}{=}R_{\hat0\hat0}-R_{\hat1\hat1}-R_{\hat2\hat2}-R_{\hat3\hat3}\). The hats denote frame components rather than coordinate labels.

title: Curvature proportional to the metric
body:
If a four-dimensional geometry has \(R_{\mu
u}=A g_{\mu
u}\), where \(A\) is a scalar, then \[R\overset{	ext{given Ricci}}{=}A g^{\mu
u}g_{\mu
u}=4A.\] The factor four counts dimensions; signature does not change the trace of the identity. In \(n\) dimensions this example gives \(nA\).

title: Cancellation loses information
body: A vanishing trace can hide nonzero Ricci components, and even zero Ricci can hide Weyl curvature. Thus \(R=0\) alone establishes neither vacuum nor flatness. Its sign also depends on the chosen curvature and metric conventions; it is not a convention-free label for attractive or repulsive gravity.

title: From scalar to action
body: The product \(R\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x\) is an invariant integration density. Its integral enters the \cref{Einstein-Hilbert action}{gr.einstein_hilbert_action}, whose variation contains the full Ricci tensor rather than only the scalar. With length-valued coordinates, \(R\) has dimensions of inverse length squared.

title: A divergence-free curvature combination
body: Ricci alone generally has a nonzero covariant divergence. Subtracting half its metric trace produces the Einstein tensor, whose divergence vanishes identically. This makes it compatible with a locally conserved stress-energy source.

title: Subtract the trace term
body:
Define \[G_{\mu
u}\coloneqq R_{\mu
u}-	frac12 Rg_{\mu
u}.\] It is symmetric for the Levi-Civita connection and depends on the metric and its derivatives through second order. The symbol \(G_{\mu
u}\) denotes a tensor; the unindexed constant \(G\) denotes Newton's gravitational constant.

title: Why one half appears
body:
The contracted \cref{Bianchi identity}{gr.bianchi_identity} gives \(
abla^\mu R_{\mu
u}=	frac12
abla_
u R\). Metric compatibility then yields \[
abla^\mu G_{\mu
u}\overset{
abla g=0}{=}
abla^\mu R_{\mu
u}-	frac12
abla_
u R\overset{	ext{Bianchi}}{=}0.\] This holds for every smooth metric with its Levi-Civita connection, before imposing any field equation.

title: The trace in four dimensions
body: Tracing the definition gives \[G^\mu{}_{\mu}=R-\tfrac12(4)R=-R.\] Consequently \(G_{\mu\nu}=0\) implies \(R=0\) and then \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\) in four dimensions. This argument changes with dimension; in two dimensions the Einstein tensor vanishes identically.

title: An identity does not determine gravity
body:
The divergence identity neither sets \(G_{\mu
u}\) to zero nor identifies it with matter. That additional physical relation is the \cref{Einstein field equation}{gr.einstein_field_equations}. A constant multiple of the metric also has zero divergence, allowing a cosmological term. Divergence-free is weaker than covariantly constant: \(
abla_ho G_{\mu
u}\) need not vanish.

title: Curvature has internal consistency
body: Curvature is built from a connection rather than specified independently at each event. Its derivatives therefore satisfy identities. The differential Bianchi identity is the one that makes the Einstein tensor's divergence vanish.

title: A cyclic differential identity
body:
For the Levi-Civita connection, \[
abla_\lambda R^ho{}_{\sigma\mu
u}+
abla_\mu R^ho{}_{\sigma
u\lambda}+
abla_
u R^ho{}_{\sigma\lambda\mu}\equiv0.\] The cyclic sum runs over the derivative index and the last two curvature indices. This is distinct from the algebraic, or first, Bianchi identity, which cycles three slots of Riemann without taking derivatives.

title: Why an identity exists
body: Covariant derivative commutators obey the Jacobi identity: the cyclic sum of nested commutators vanishes. Inserting their curvature action gives the differential identity above. Equivalently, in normal coordinates the relevant second derivatives of the connection cancel cyclically. Neither route uses matter properties or Einstein's equations.

title: Contract to a useful form
body:
Contracting with the metric and using Riemann's symmetries produces \[2
abla^\mu R_{\mu
u}-
abla_
u R\equiv0.\] By the definition of the \cref{Einstein tensor}{gr.einstein_tensor} and metric compatibility this becomes \(
abla^\mu G_{\mu
u}\equiv0\). The contraction hides much of the original index structure while retaining the identity needed for source consistency.

title: Geometry and matter play different roles
body:
For constant \(\Lambda\), both \(G_{\mu
u}\) and \(\Lambda g_{\mu
u}\) are divergence-free. Applying the field equation then requires \(
abla^\mu T_{\mu
u}=0\). This is a compatibility statement about a coupled solution; the geometric identity alone is not a matter equation of motion or a guarantee of a globally conserved total energy.

title: Test geometry rather than chart components
body: A component can diverge because coordinates fail. Scalar contractions of curvature take the same value at an event in every regular chart, so their divergence is stronger evidence of a geometric problem.

title: Useful contractions
body:
Common examples are the Ricci scalar \(R\), the squared Ricci contraction \(R_{\mu
u}R^{\mu
u}\), and the Kretschmann scalar \[K\coloneqq R_{\mu
uho\sigma}R^{\mu
uho\sigma}.\] All indices are contracted with the metric. Despite the language of a square, such Lorentzian contractions need not be positive for arbitrary tensors or geometries.

title: Schwarzschild separates two suspect radii
body: For Schwarzschild with \(m\coloneqq GM/c^2\), direct curvature evaluation gives \[R\overset{\text{vacuum}}{=}0,\qquad K\overset{\text{Schwarzschild}}{=}\frac{48m^2}{r^6}.\] Thus the apparent metric divergence at \(r=2m\) has finite \(K=3/(4m^4)\), whereas \(K\) diverges as \(r\to0\). The first is a chart failure that a regular extension removes; the second is divergent tidal curvature.

title: Check dimensions and scale
body: Since curvature has dimensions of inverse length squared, \(K\) has dimensions of inverse length to the fourth power. Doubling \(r\) at fixed mass reduces Schwarzschild's \(K\) by 64. This quantifies local curvature, not the strength of a coordinate acceleration or the existence of a horizon.

title: A diagnostic is not a complete regularity theorem
body: Finite scalar invariants do not prove extendibility or geodesic completeness, and some curved Lorentzian geometries have vanishing polynomial curvature invariants. A complete singularity analysis examines causal geodesics and possible extensions. See \cref{coordinate singularity}{gr.coordinate_singularity} and \cref{black-hole singularity}{gr.black_hole_singularity} for the Schwarzschild distinction.

title: Let the metric be dynamical
body: A particle action varies a path in a given metric. The Einstein-Hilbert action instead varies the metric itself, providing field equations for spacetime geometry. Matter contributes its own action to the same stationary-variation problem.

title: Keep action and curvature signs together
body: Use \(c\overset{\text{units}}{=}1\), \(\kappa\coloneqq8\pi G\), signature \(+---\), and the atlas Riemann convention. Define \[S_g\coloneqq-\frac{1}{2\kappa}\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,(R+2\Lambda).\] This pairs with \(\delta S_m=\tfrac12\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,T_{\mu\nu}\delta g^{\mu\nu}\). Other consistent conventions use different signs; copying the action alone from them changes the theory's relative coupling.

title: Two variations make the Einstein tensor
body:
Varying the inverse metric gives \(\delta\sqrt{-g}=-	frac12\sqrt{-g}\,g_{\mu
u}\delta g^{\mu
u}\) and \(\delta R=R_{\mu
u}\delta g^{\mu
u}+g^{\mu
u}\delta R_{\mu
u}\). The last term is a divergence. Hence, for variations of compact support, \[\delta S_g\overset{	ext{boundary vanishes}}{=}- rac{1}{2\kappa}\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,(G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u})\delta g^{\mu
u}.\] The determinant variation supplies the trace term that Ricci alone lacks.

title: Stationarity supplies the field equation
body:
Adding the matter variation and requiring \(\delta(S_g+S_m)\overset{	ext{stationary}}{=}0\) for arbitrary interior metric variations yields \[G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{metric variation}}{=}\kappa T_{\mu
u}.\] The gravitational action selects dynamics; the Bianchi identity checks their consistency. See \cref{stress-energy variation}{gr.stress_energy_variation} for the source definition.

title: Boundary conditions are part of the problem
body: Compactly supported variations justify the local derivation above. On a region with a boundary, fixing only the induced metric does not generally remove the normal derivatives of its variation from the bare action. A suitable gravitational boundary term is then required. The cosmological term is optional physics, while the boundary treatment is necessary for the stated variational problem.

title: The local source of curvature
body: Stress-energy packages the energy and momentum carried by matter and non-gravitational fields. GR places this tensor on curved spacetime and couples it to geometry. The \cref{SR energy-momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor} develops its flat-spacetime role; the two concepts remain separate but linked.

title: What an observer measures
body: For an observer with four-velocity \(v\), normalised by \(g(v,v)=c^2\), define the measured energy density \[\epsilon_{(v)}\coloneqq\frac{1}{c^2}T_{\mu\nu}v^\mu v^\nu.\] This contraction is a scalar once the observer is specified. Different observers can measure different densities at the same event without disagreeing about the tensor.

title: Components in a local rest frame
body: In an orthonormal frame with \(x^{\hat0}=ct\), \(T^{\hat0\hat0}\) is energy density, \(cT^{\hat0\hat i}\) is energy flux and \(T^{\hat i\hat j}\) is momentum flux or stress. Symmetry relates energy flux to momentum density. These interpretations apply to orthonormal components; arbitrary coordinate components need the appropriate frame factors.

title: More than rest mass gravitates
body: Pressure, radiation and field energy all contribute to \(T_{\mu\nu}\). A \cref{perfect fluid}{gr.perfect_fluid} provides a simple model, while \cref{metric variation of matter}{gr.stress_energy_variation} supplies a general construction. The source includes all interacting matter sectors together; one sector may exchange energy with another.

title: Do not add a local gravity tensor by analogy
body: The right-hand source in Einstein's equation is not a general local tensor density of gravitational energy. Gravitational dynamics also reside in the metric's nonlinear field equation. Accordingly \cref{covariant conservation}{gr.covariant_conservation} does not by itself provide a conserved total energy for every spacetime.

title: Isotropy defines the idealisation
body: A perfect fluid has a local rest frame with energy density \(\epsilon\), isotropic pressure \(p\), and no heat flux or viscous stress. Its continuum description is useful when a small fluid element contains many particles yet is small compared with macroscopic gradients.

title: Build the covariant tensor
body:
With signature \(+---\) and \(g(u,u)=c^2\), the model is \[T^{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{perfect fluid}}{=} rac{\epsilon+p}{c^2}u^\mu u^
u-pg^{\mu
u}.\] In the local fluid rest frame, \(u^{\hat\mu}=(c,0,0,0)\), so \(T^{\hat\mu\hat
u}=\mathrm{diag}(\epsilon,p,p,p)\). The minus metric term gives positive spatial pressures in this signature.

title: Dust and radiation
body: Dust neglects pressure and gives \(T^{\mu\nu}=\epsilon u^\mu u^\nu/c^2\), with \(\epsilon\simeq\rho c^2\) when rest mass dominates. Isotropic radiation instead has \(p=\epsilon/3\). Both fit the same tensor form, but their matter response differs through their \cref{equation of state}{gr.equation_of_state}.

title: Project conservation along the flow
body:
Contract \(
abla_\mu T^{\mu
u}=0\) with \(u_
u\). Metric compatibility and fixed velocity norm remove the acceleration contraction, leaving \[u^\mu
abla_\mu\epsilon+(\epsilon+p)
abla_\mu u^\mu\overset{	ext{energy balance}}{=}0.\] The first term follows a fluid element's density; the second accounts for expansion and pressure work. Projecting perpendicular to \(u\) gives the fluid acceleration caused by pressure gradients.

title: Perfect does not mean pressureless or geodesic
body: The absence of viscosity is not the absence of pressure. Pressure gradients can accelerate the fluid, so its elements need not follow geodesics. Freely moving dust does follow geodesics wherever its density is nonzero, until effects such as stream crossing invalidate a single-fluid velocity description.

title: State the matter assumptions of a theorem
body: Energy conditions impose inequalities on stress-energy. They make assumptions such as nonnegative observer energy or causal energy flow precise. They are additional hypotheses, not identities or consequences of Einstein's equations.

title: Null and weak conditions
body:
The null energy condition (NEC) requires \(T_{\mu
u}k^\mu k^
u\geq0\) for every null \(k\). The weak energy condition (WEC) requires \(T_{\mu
u}v^\mu v^
u\geq0\) for every timelike \(v\). Normalising \(v\) turns the latter into nonnegative measured energy density. By continuity WEC implies NEC.

title: Dominant and strong conditions
body:
With \(+---\), the dominant energy condition (DEC) requires \(J^\mu\coloneqq T^\mu{}_{
u}v^
u\) to be future-directed causal or zero for every future timelike \(v\). The strong energy condition (SEC) requires \((T_{\mu
u}-	frac12Tg_{\mu
u})v^\mu v^
u\geq0\) in four dimensions. Through the field equations with zero cosmological constant, SEC gives the Ricci convergence condition used in focusing arguments. With \(\Lambda
e0\), include its effective source before drawing that conclusion.

title: Perfect-fluid tests
body: For a perfect fluid the conditions reduce to: NEC, \(\epsilon+p\geq0\); WEC, also \(\epsilon\geq0\); DEC, \(\epsilon\geq|p|\); SEC, \(\epsilon+p\geq0\) and \(\epsilon+3p\geq0\). These follow by testing rest-frame and highly boosted observers. Positive vacuum energy has \(p=-\epsilon\), so it satisfies NEC, WEC and DEC but violates SEC.

title: Names do not form a strength ranking
body: The strong condition is not stronger than the weak condition in the logical sense. Classical models can violate some conditions, and quantum expectation values can violate pointwise conditions too. A theorem using one remains conditional on that precise assumption; failure of the assumption alone neither proves nor disproves the theorem's conclusion.

title: Balance includes geometric comparison
body: Local energy-momentum balance must compare tensor quantities at neighbouring events. In curved spacetime the connection supplies that comparison. For the total matter source with its equations of motion satisfied, the conservation statement is \(\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0\).

title: Expand the divergence
body:
The tensor derivative gives \[
abla_\mu T^{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu T^{\mu
u}+\Gamma^\mu{}_{\mu\lambda}T^{\lambda
u}+\Gamma^
u{}_{\mu\lambda}T^{\mu\lambda}.\] The two connection terms act on different indices. They can be removed at one event in a local inertial chart, but not generally across a finite region. Even flat spacetime needs them in curvilinear coordinates.

title: Consistency of the coupled equations
body:
For constant \(\Lambda\), taking the divergence of Einstein's equation gives \[\kappa
abla^\mu T_{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{EFE}}{=}
abla^\mu G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda
abla^\mu g_{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{Bianchi, compatibility}}{=}0.\] The same matter conservation follows from diffeomorphism invariance of the matter action when the matter fields obey their equations. A subsystem exchanging energy with other fields need not be separately conserved.

title: A symmetry can supply a conserved charge
body:
If a vector field \(\xi\) generates an isometry, it obeys the Killing equation \(
abla_\mu\xi_
u+
abla_
u\xi_\mu=0\). Symmetry of stress-energy then makes \(J^\mu\coloneqq T^{\mu
u}\xi_
u\) divergence-free. Integrating this vector current gives a conserved charge when boundary flux vanishes. A timelike symmetry supplies an energy interpretation.

title: Local balance is not universal global energy
body: A generic spacetime has no time-translation symmetry. One cannot simply add coordinate energy components at different events and infer a conserved total from the tensor divergence. Boundary or asymptotic constructions can provide gravitational energy in appropriate settings, but require additional structure.

title: Supply material physics
body: Einstein's equations couple geometry to matter but do not specify how a material's pressure depends on its thermodynamic state. An equation of state supplies this constitutive information. Together with conservation and a fluid model, it closes the evolution problem.

title: A simple barotropic model
body: A barotropic fluid assumes \(p=p(\epsilon)\), where \(\epsilon\) is rest-frame energy density. A useful idealisation is the model law \[p=w\epsilon,\qquad w\coloneqq p/\epsilon\quad(\epsilon\ne0).\] The first equation assumes constant \(w\) when used as a linear equation of state; the ratio definition alone does not assert that constancy. Pressure and energy density have the same units.

title: Three distinct responses
body: Pressureless dust uses \(w=0\); isotropic radiation uses \(w=1/3\); an effective cosmological source uses \(w=-1\). The last is not an ordinary gas with a preferred fluid rest frame. These examples are material assumptions or idealisations, rather than alternatives to the gravitational field equation.

title: Count the missing relation
body: On a given metric, a perfect fluid has energy density, pressure and three independent velocity components. Its four conservation equations leave one constitutive relation to supply. More general materials need additional variables such as particle density, entropy or composition, with their own equations; a single barotropic relation is then insufficient.

title: Sound speed is a derivative
body: For adiabatic perturbations of a suitable ordinary fluid, \(c_s^2=c^2(\partial p/\partial\epsilon)_s\), where entropy per particle is held fixed. Thus a constant barotropic law gives \(c_s^2=wc^2\). Stability and causal propagation constrain the derivative, not just the ratio \(p/\epsilon\). Do not interpret the vacuum relation \(w=-1\) as the sound speed of an ordinary fluid.

title: Couple geometry and matter
body: Einstein's equations determine how the metric responds to matter and non-gravitational fields. The metric also controls matter motion, so this is a coupled system rather than a one-way force prescription.

title: The atlas field equation
body:
With signature \(+---\), the glossary's Riemann definition and explicit \(c\), define \(\kappa\coloneqq8\pi G/c^4\). The field equation is \[G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}=\kappa T_{\mu
u}.\] The minus sign before \(\Lambda\) belongs to this complete convention; positive \(\Lambda\) represents positive effective vacuum energy. Sources using the opposite signature often write a plus sign. Comparing signs requires comparing curvature definitions too.

title: Why this combination works
body: The \cref{Einstein tensor}{gr.einstein_tensor} and constant metric term have zero covariant divergence. Their source must therefore obey \cref{covariant conservation}{gr.covariant_conservation}. The coupling is fixed by recovering Newton's Poisson equation for weak, slowly varying fields and nonrelativistic matter. Pressure and radiation remain sources beyond that limit.

title: Equations need data and a matter model
body: There are ten symmetric component equations in four dimensions, linked by four differential identities and coordinate freedom. Their initial-value formulation contains constraints as well as evolution equations. Solving requires appropriate initial or boundary data, a coordinate choice and matter dynamics; conservation alone does not select a unique spacetime.

title: Vacuum is not the absence of gravitational physics
body: Where \(T_{\mu\nu}=0\), curvature can still encode tides and gravitational waves. Nonlinear metric terms describe gravitational self-interaction without inserting a universal local gravitational stress-energy tensor on the right. The \cref{trace-reversed form}{gr.trace_reversed_equations} is often easier for calculations but describes the same theory.

title: A uniform geometric term
body: The cosmological constant \(\Lambda\) permits curvature even without ordinary matter. It has dimensions of inverse length squared and multiplies the metric, introducing no preferred observer direction at an event.

title: Move it to an effective source
body:
In our convention \(G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}=\kappa T_{\mu
u}\). Equivalently, \[G_{\mu
u}=\kappa(T_{\mu
u}+T^{(\Lambda)}_{\mu
u}),\qquad T^{(\Lambda)}_{\mu
u}\coloneqq rac{\Lambda}{\kappa}g_{\mu
u}.\] This is an algebraic reassignment, not additional matter counted twice. If vacuum energy is already included in \(T\), its contribution must not also be repeated in \(\Lambda\).

title: Read its density and pressure
body: Comparing with the perfect-fluid form gives \[\epsilon_\Lambda\overset{\text{observer projection}}{=}\frac{\Lambda c^4}{8\pi G},\qquad p_\Lambda=-\epsilon_\Lambda.\] The combination \(\epsilon_\Lambda+p_\Lambda\) vanishes, removing dependence on a fluid velocity. Positive \(\Lambda\) therefore gives the same positive vacuum density to every timelike observer.

title: Curved empty spacetime
body: In four-dimensional ordinary vacuum, tracing the field equation gives \(R=-4\Lambda\) and hence \(R_{\mu\nu}=-\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}\) in our convention. Positive \(\Lambda\) permits de Sitter geometry and contributes an outward acceleration \(\Lambda c^2r/3\) in the weak static spherical limit. The sign of the Ricci scalar alone must not be used to infer attraction.

title: The equation does not explain the value
body: A metric-proportional source can model vacuum energy, but classical GR does not determine its microscopic origin or numerical value. Cosmological observations and quantum vacuum-energy calculations are separate subjects. A spacetime-varying replacement needs extra dynamics or energy exchange to remain compatible with the Bianchi identity.

title: Measure matter's response to geometry
body: Changing the metric changes distances, volume and the contractions in a matter action. The coefficient of that variation defines the Hilbert stress-energy tensor. This construction makes its role as the gravitational source explicit.

title: Vary the inverse metric
body:
Use \(c\overset{	ext{units}}{=}1\), signature \(+---\), and hold the matter fields fixed during metric variation. Define \[T_{\mu
u}\coloneqq rac{2}{\sqrt{-g}} rac{\delta S_m}{\delta g^{\mu
u}},\qquad\delta S_m= rac12\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,T_{\mu
u}\delta g^{\mu
u}.\] The functional derivative includes integrations by parts where required. This plus sign pairs with the negative gravitational action in the glossary.

title: A minimally coupled scalar example
body:
Take \(S_m=\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,\mathcal L_m\), where \(\mathcal L_m\coloneqq	frac12g^{\alpha eta}\partial_\alpha\phi\partial_ eta\phi-V(\phi)\). Varying both the contraction and the determinant gives \[T_{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{metric variation}}{=}\partial_\mu\phi\partial_
u\phi-g_{\mu
u}\mathcal L_m.\] The first contribution comes from \(g^{\alpha eta}\); the second from \(\sqrt{-g}\). Omitting the volume variation gives the wrong source.

title: Check physical energy
body: In a local orthonormal frame the scalar example gives \[T_{\hat0\hat0}=\tfrac12(\partial_{\hat0}\phi)^2+\tfrac12\sum_i(\partial_{\hat i}\phi)^2+V(\phi).\] For a nonnegative potential the measured energy density is nonnegative. This is a useful sign check against the chosen action, although it does not establish every energy condition.

title: Changing the varied variable changes a sign
body:
Because \(\delta g^{\mu
u}=-g^{\mu\alpha}g^{
u eta}\delta g_{\alpha eta}\), varying the covariant metric instead gives \(\delta S_m=-	frac12\int\sqrt{-g}\,T^{\mu
u}\delta g_{\mu
u}\,d^4x\). Symmetry of the metric variation gives a symmetric tensor. Its covariant conservation additionally uses the matter equations, not merely this definition.

title: Solve algebraically for Ricci
body: Trace reversal rewrites Einstein's equations as a direct relation between Ricci curvature and a trace-adjusted source. It changes the algebraic packaging, not the theory, and is particularly useful in the Newtonian and vacuum limits.

title: Take the four-dimensional trace
body:
Define \(T\coloneqq g^{\mu
u}T_{\mu
u}\). Starting with the atlas equation and using \(g^{\mu
u}g_{\mu
u}=4\), \[R-2R-4\Lambda\overset{	ext{traced EFE}}{=}\kappa T,\qquad R=-\kappa T-4\Lambda.\] The factor four is dimensional, not a consequence of the signature.

title: Substitute the trace back
body:
Rearrange the original equation as \(R_{\mu
u}=\kappa T_{\mu
u}+	frac12Rg_{\mu
u}+\Lambda g_{\mu
u}\). Substituting the trace gives \[R_{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{trace substitution}}{=}\kappa\left(T_{\mu
u}-	frac12Tg_{\mu
u}ight)-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}.\] The minus cosmological sign agrees with the glossary. The adjusted source need not share all physical interpretations of the original stress-energy tensor.

title: Pressure remains in the source
body: For a perfect fluid in its orthonormal rest frame, \(T=\epsilon-3p\). Therefore \[R_{\hat0\hat0}\overset{\text{perfect fluid}}{=}\frac{\kappa}{2}(\epsilon+3p)-\Lambda.\] This helps explain why relativistic pressure gravitates. It is a local curvature relation, not by itself an equation for a star's total mass.

title: The coefficient depends on dimension
body: In \(n>2\) dimensions the source trace coefficient is \(1/(n-2)\), and the cosmological term here is \(-2\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}/(n-2)\). The familiar one half is specific to four dimensions. In two dimensions this inversion fails because the Einstein tensor vanishes identically.

title: Remove matter locally, not curvature
body: An ordinary vacuum region has \(T_{\mu\nu}=0\). It can lie outside a star or black hole even though matter elsewhere helped determine its geometry. Vacuum is a local source condition, not a statement that nothing gravitational happens there.

title: Zero cosmological constant
body: In four dimensions with \(\Lambda=0\), the field equation gives \(G_{\mu\nu}=0\). Taking the trace yields \(R=0\), so \[R_{\mu\nu}\overset{\text{vacuum EFE}}{=}0.\] This is Ricci-flatness. It constrains a contraction of Riemann, leaving possible Weyl curvature and tidal effects.

title: Schwarzschild is curved vacuum
body: Outside a spherical body the Schwarzschild solution has zero Ricci tensor but \(K=48(GM/c^2)^2/r^6\). Thus a freely falling cloud can deform despite the absence of local matter. \cref{Gravitational waves}{gr.gravitational_waves} also illustrate vacuum curvature carrying physical tidal information.

title: Retaining the cosmological term
body:
With ordinary matter absent but \(\Lambda
e0\), the atlas trace-reversed equation instead gives \[R_{\mu
u}\overset{T_{\mu
u}=0}{=}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}.\] This is not Ricci-flat. State whether vacuum includes an explicit cosmological term or whether that term has been absorbed into an effective stress-energy source.

title: Vacuum equations do not select Schwarzschild alone
body: A solution still needs symmetry assumptions and suitable data. Schwarzschild describes spherical vacuum with zero cosmological constant; rotating or time-dependent vacuum geometries need not share its form. Boundary conditions retain information about sources outside the region in which the vacuum equation is being solved.

title: Approximate a region by a flat background
body: Weak-field theory describes a metric close to Minkowski form across a useful region in suitable coordinates. This is stronger than local flatness at one event and does not require that all sources or test particles move slowly.

title: Choose a background split
body:
Define the perturbation by \(h_{\mu
u}\coloneqq g_{\mu
u}-\eta_{\mu
u}\), with \(|h_{\mu
u}|\ll1\) in the chosen background chart. To first order, \[g^{\mu
u}\simeq\eta^{\mu
u}-h^{\mu
u},\qquad h^{\mu
u}\coloneqq\eta^{\mu\alpha}\eta^{
u eta}h_{\alpha eta}.\] Multiplying this inverse by \(g_{\mu
u}\) cancels the linear correction; products of perturbations are discarded.

title: Connection and curvature at first order
body:
The Levi-Civita formula becomes \[\Gamma^ho{}_{\mu
u}\simeq	frac12\eta^{ho\sigma}(\partial_\mu h_{\sigma
u}+\partial_
u h_{\sigma\mu}-\partial_\sigma h_{\mu
u}).\] Curvature contains second derivatives of \(h\) at this order; the quadratic connection terms enter later. Small metric amplitude need not mean slow time variation, as weak gravitational waves illustrate.

title: A static Newtonian source
body: For slowly moving matter with negligible pressure and anisotropic stress, a convenient isotropic weak-field chart gives \[ds^2\simeq(1+2\Phi/c^2)c^2dt^2-(1-2\Phi/c^2)\delta_{ij}dx^i dx^j.\] Here \(\Phi\) is the Newtonian potential and \(\Lambda\) is neglected. Both time and spatial components change; ignoring the latter loses part of the light-deflection result.

title: Gauge and approximation are different choices
body: A small coordinate change changes the components of \(h\), so their smallness is assessed in an appropriate chart, not every possible chart. Linearisation discards nonlinear terms after that choice. The \cref{Newtonian limit}{gr.newtonian_limit} adds slow motion and approximate stationarity; the \cref{post-Newtonian scheme}{gr.post_newtonian_approximation} keeps selected nonlinear terms consistently.

title: Recover both motion and the source law
body: The Newtonian limit requires a weak, approximately stationary field, slow test bodies and nonrelativistic sources whose pressure is small compared with rest energy. Set \(\Lambda=0\) for the ordinary Poisson law. Recovering acceleration alone is only half the check.

title: The metric gives the force law
body: With \(x^0=ct\) and \(g_{00}\simeq1+2\Phi/c^2\), the static connection gives \(\Gamma^i{}_{00}\simeq\partial_i\Phi/c^2\). The dominant part of the spatial geodesic equation is therefore \[\frac{d^2x^i}{dt^2}\simeq-c^2\Gamma^i{}_{00}\simeq-\partial_i\Phi.\] Slow motion suppresses terms involving spatial velocities; weak fields let proper time and coordinate time agree to the required order.

title: The field equation gives Poisson's law
body:
For a static weak perturbation, \(R_{00}\simeq
abla^2\Phi/c^2\). For low-pressure matter, \(T_{00}\simeqho c^2\) and \(T\simeqho c^2\), where \(ho\) is mass density. The \cref{trace-reversed equation}{gr.trace_reversed_equations} then gives \[ rac{
abla^2\Phi}{c^2}\simeq rac{\kappa}{2}ho c^2,\qquad
abla^2\Phi\simeq4\pi Gho.\] This fixes \(\kappa=8\pi G/c^4\) by matching Newtonian gravity.

title: An isolated spherical source
body: Outside the source, spherical symmetry and zero potential at infinity give \(\Phi=-GM/r\) in Newtonian theory. Its gradient produces inward acceleration \(-GM\mathbf x/r^3\). Inserting this potential into \(g_{00}\) also predicts the leading slowing of stationary clocks nearer the mass.

title: Keep the limits distinct
body: Small potential does not make light slow or radiation pressure negligible. The Newtonian motion approximation fails for light, even when linearised gravity remains valid. If \(\Lambda\) is retained, the same convention gives \(\nabla^2\Phi\simeq4\pi G\rho-\Lambda c^2\); the ordinary inverse-square result assumes that extra term is negligible.

title: Compare emission and reception clocks
body: A light signal exchanged by stationary observers in a static gravitational field can have different measured frequencies at its endpoints. The comparison concerns their proper-time rates; each observer still measures local vacuum light speed \(c\).

title: Stationary proper-time rates
body: Write the static metric with \(x^0=ct\), zero time-space cross terms, and \(g_{00}>0\) along the stationary observers. At fixed spatial coordinates, \[d\tau\overset{\text{stationary observer}}{=}\sqrt{g_{00}}\,dt.\] The common coordinate time is tied to the static symmetry; it is not itself the reading of every clock.

title: Use successive wave crests
body: Time-translation symmetry makes successive crests take the same coordinate travel time, so their emission and reception coordinate intervals agree. Dividing by the local proper-time rates gives \[\frac{\nu_B}{\nu_A}\overset{\text{static exchange}}{=}\sqrt{\frac{g_{00}(A)}{g_{00}(B)}}.\] Here \(A\) emits and \(B\) receives. This static formula is exact, not restricted to a weak field.

title: A small height difference
Do not apply the static formula to arbitrary observers
body: Motion adds Doppler effects, and a time-dependent geometry need not preserve the coordinate interval argument. Even a static chart ceases to describe physical stationary observers where its time direction becomes null or spacelike, as at and inside a Schwarzschild horizon. The conserved photon quantity associated with time symmetry is distinct from the energy measured by each local observer.

title: Follow null geodesics
body: In geometric optics, freely propagating light follows null geodesics of the metric. A weak isolated mass changes their direction relative to distant incoming and outgoing reference lines. No photon rest mass or material refractive medium is required.

title: The weak scattering setup
body: Take a static spherical mass \(M\), source and observer far away, and impact parameter \(b\) with \(GM/(bc^2)\ll1\). The impact parameter is the offset of the incoming asymptotic line, equal to closest approach only at leading order. Ignore rotation, other masses and cosmological curvature.

title: The full weak metric doubles the gradient term
body: From the isotropic weak-field metric and \(ds^2=0\), \(c\,dt\simeq(1-2\Phi/c^2)d\ell\). Thus the coordinate optical path has an effective index \(n\simeq1-2\Phi/c^2\). This is a computational description of geometry, not a local change in light speed. The transverse ray change is \(\Delta\mathbf e_\perp\simeq-2c^{-2}\int\nabla_\perp\Phi\,dz\) along the unperturbed line.

title: Integrate a point-mass potential
body: For \(\Phi=-GM/\sqrt{b^2+z^2}\), the magnitude of the leading bending is \[\alpha\simeq\frac{2GMb}{c^2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dz}{(b^2+z^2)^{3/2}}=\frac{4GM}{bc^2}.\] The ray bends towards the mass. In this chart, the time and spatial metric perturbations each supply half; that split is coordinate-dependent while the asymptotic deflection is observable.

title: Stay outside the strong-deflection regime
body: The result is first order in \(GM/(bc^2)\). Close to the photon sphere, multiple turns and capture require the full null-geodesic equations. A \cref{Newtonian slow-body calculation}{gr.newtonian_limit} cannot be applied to light to obtain the missing spatial contribution.

title: Radial and angular periods separate
body: In Newtonian inverse-square gravity, a bound test orbit is a closed ellipse. Schwarzschild geodesics add a small mismatch between radial oscillation and angular revolution, so the closest-approach direction advances. For other central bodies the same effect is called periapsis advance.

title: The orbit equation exposes the correction
body: Use \(m\coloneqq GM/c^2\), a test body, spherical nonrotating geometry and \(\Lambda=0\). Let \(q\coloneqq1/r\) and \(\ell\coloneqq r^2d\phi/d\tau\) be specific angular momentum. The timelike Schwarzschild geodesic equation reduces to \[\frac{d^2q}{d\phi^2}+q\overset{\text{Schwarzschild geodesic}}{=}\frac{GM}{\ell^2}+3mq^2.\] The last term is absent from the Kepler problem. The inverse radius is called \(q\) here to avoid confusing it with four-velocity \(u^\mu\).

title: Find the frequency shift
body: Write the leading ellipse as \(q_0=(1+e\cos\phi)/p_{\mathrm{orb}}\), with \(p_{\mathrm{orb}}\coloneqq a(1-e^2)\). Substitution into \(3mq_0^2\) produces a resonant \(\cos\phi\) term. Absorbing it into \(q\simeq[1+e\cos((1-\delta)\phi)]/p_{\mathrm{orb}}\) gives \(\delta\simeq3m/p_{\mathrm{orb}}\). Two periapses are therefore separated by slightly more than \(2\pi\).

title: Advance per radial orbit
body: The leading extra angle is \[\Delta\varpi\simeq\frac{6\pi GM}{a(1-e^2)c^2}.\] Here \(a\) and \(e\) are the leading Keplerian semimajor axis and eccentricity. The approximation requires a weak field throughout the orbit, especially near periapsis; the advance is positive for the Schwarzschild correction.

title: Separate other causes of precession
body: Other planets, a nonspherical central body and spin can also rotate the periapsis. The displayed expression isolates the test-body Schwarzschild contribution and omits radiation reaction. An exactly circular orbit has no unique periapsis direction; the nearly circular limit describes the mismatch between radial and angular frequencies.

title: Order corrections to slow orbital motion
body: Post-Newtonian (PN) theory extends Newtonian gravity with a controlled expansion for slow motion and a weak orbital field. It retains the nonlinear terms required at each order, unlike a calculation restricted to first order in the metric perturbation.

title: Choose an order-counting parameter
body: For a gravitationally bound system define \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}\coloneqq v^2/c^2\ll1\). Virial scaling makes \(GM/(rc^2)\) of the same order. Newtonian dynamics is called 0PN; relative corrections of order \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}^2\) are 1PN and 2PN. This is order counting, not an exact equality between velocity and potential for every orbit.

title: Keep a consistent collection of terms
body: Obtaining 1PN motion generally needs \(g_{00}\) through order \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}^2\), \(g_{0i}\) through order \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}^{3/2}\), and spatial corrections through order \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}\) in suitable coordinates. The components enter the motion equation multiplied by different velocity factors. Keeping the same power in every component would therefore miss contributions.

title: Conservative and dissipative corrections
body: Periapsis advance appears at 1PN. For nonspinning compact binaries, leading radiation reaction enters orbital motion at 2.5PN, relative order \((v/c)^5\), and causes secular energy loss. PN orders in a waveform or flux are counted relative to their own leading terms, so they should not be confused with orders in the acceleration.

title: Know the domain of the expansion
body: Near a merger or a horizon, slow-motion orbital expansion loses control. Widely separated compact bodies can nevertheless be treated using effective body descriptions even when their internal gravity is strong. Coordinate-dependent intermediate formulas must be compared using observables at the same retained order; more terms alone do not guarantee accuracy outside the approximation's regime. The orbital expansion describes the near zone; radiation at large distances requires matching to a wave-zone solution.

title: Ripples of the metric
body: Gravitational waves are propagating disturbances of spacetime geometry. In the \cref{Weak-field metric}{gr.weak_field_metric} description they are small, time-dependent metric perturbations travelling through a region that may be ordinary vacuum. They are not waves in a material medium; the geometry itself carries the changing tidal field.

title: Weak vacuum wave
body:
Write \(g_{\mu
u}=\eta_{\mu
u}+h_{\mu
u}\) with \(|h_{\mu
u}|\ll1\). In a suitable linearized gauge, the source-free field equations reduce schematically to \[ \Box  ar h_{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{vacuum linearized EFE}}{=}0, \] where \( ar h_{\mu
u}\) is the \cref{trace-reversed}{gr.trace_reversed_equations} perturbation. This wave equation is a weak-field statement; it is not the full nonlinear Einstein equation.

title: What the wave does
body: A passing wave changes the relative separations of freely falling test masses transverse to its direction of travel. The observable is strain, \(h\sim\Delta L/L\), not a force pushing all objects together in the same way. This is the same tidal logic as \cref{Geodesic deviation}{gr.geodesic_deviation}, applied to a travelling curvature pattern.

title: Two transverse patterns
body: Far from sources in the transverse-traceless description, a wave travelling in one direction has two independent polarisation patterns, often called \(+\) and \(\times\). They alternately stretch and squeeze perpendicular directions. These labels describe the physical tidal pattern after gauge freedom has been fixed, not arbitrary coordinate wiggles.

title: Changing quadrupoles radiate
body: Spherical pulsation does not radiate gravitational waves in GR; a changing quadrupole-like mass distribution is the leading source. Compact binaries are the central example: their near-zone motion can be treated with \cref{Post-Newtonian approximation}{gr.post_newtonian_approximation} when widely separated, while the outgoing radiation is read in the wave zone.

title: Not sound in space
body: Gravitational waves can pass through vacuum because they are solutions of the gravitational field equations, not pressure waves in matter. Conversely, a small coordinate ripple is not automatically a physical wave. The physical content is the gauge-invariant tidal effect that remains in detector separations.

title: An exact spherical vacuum solution
body: Schwarzschild geometry solves the vacuum Einstein equations with zero cosmological constant and spherical symmetry. Its exterior is static even if a spherical source pulsates: this is the content of Birkhoff's theorem. Rotation, electromagnetic stress outside a charged body, or nonspherical radiation require other geometries.

title: Coordinates and signature
body: With \(+---\), define \(m\coloneqq GM/c^2\), \(f(r)\coloneqq1-2m/r\), and \(d\Omega^2\coloneqq d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\). The line element is \[ds^2=f(r)c^2dt^2-f(r)^{-1}dr^2-r^2d\Omega^2.\] The time coordinate is normalised to proper time of stationary observers at infinity. The exterior chart requires \(r>2m\).

title: Deriving the spherical vacuum metric
body:
The \cref{vacuum equations}{gr.vacuum_field_equations} determine the radial dependence; spherical symmetry alone does not. On a static exterior patch, use areal radius and write \(ds^2=A(r)c^2dt^2-B(r)dr^2-r^2d\Omega^2\), with \(A,B>0\) and \(\Lambda=0\). Solving \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\) gives \(B^{-1}=1-C/r\) and \(AB=D\), where \(C,D\) are constants. Normalising time at infinity sets \(D=1\). The large-radius comparison with the Newtonian potential identifies \(C=2GM/c^2\), giving the displayed Schwarzschild metric.

\optional_details{Two radial equations}{Independent combinations of the vacuum equations reduce to \[\frac{d}{dr}\left[r\left(1-\frac1B\right)\right]=0,\qquad \frac{d}{dr}\ln(AB)=0.\] The first integrates to \(r(1-B^{-1})=C\); the second gives \(AB=D\). Hence \(A=D(1-C/r)\). With \(D=1\), comparing \(A\) with \(1+2\Phi/c^2\) and \(\Phi=-GM/r\) fixes the mass constant. The remaining vacuum component is then satisfied. This derives the static exterior solution; Birkhoff's stronger result explains why spherical vacuum symmetry suffices even when the source pulsates. It does not assert that the black-hole interior is static.}

title: Areal radius is not radial ruler distance
body: A symmetry sphere has area \(4\pi r^2\), which defines the geometric meaning of \(r\). Along a radial line on an exterior constant-time slice, the proper distance element is \(d\ell=dr/\sqrt{f}\). Thus coordinate radius is not generally the distance a chain of local rulers measures from a centre.

title: Read the weak-field limit
body: At large radius, \(f=1+2\Phi/c^2\) with \(\Phi=-GM/r\), recovering the Newtonian time component. The spatial part tends to flat spherical coordinates as \(r\to\infty\). At finite radius, the exact metric retains the nonlinear geometry needed for horizons and relativistic orbit structure.

title: A solution and its chart have different limits
body: An ordinary star's interior is not vacuum, so its material surface ends the exterior solution's physical applicability. For a black hole, \(r=2m\) is a failure of these coordinates; a \cref{regular extension}{gr.coordinate_singularity} crosses it. The singularity at \(r=0\) is a different, invariant problem. The static exterior description does not make the black-hole interior static.

title: Mass sets a length scale
body: The Schwarzschild radius translates a physical mass into a characteristic relativistic length. It locates the horizon of a Schwarzschild black hole, but exists as a useful mass scale even for bodies whose surfaces lie far outside it.

title: The zero of the exterior lapse factor
body: Define \[r_s\coloneqq\frac{2GM}{c^2}=2m.\] The factor \(f(r)=1-r_s/r\) vanishes at this radius. The factors \(G\) and \(c\) convert mass to length: \([GM/c^2]=\mathrm{length}\). Doubling mass doubles the radius.

title: Compare scale with material size
body: For \(M\simeq2.0\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}\), using \(G\simeq6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\) and \(c\simeq3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), \(r_s\simeq3.0\,\mathrm{km}\). A star of this mass can have a much larger material radius, so its exterior region never reaches this formal zero.

title: Compactness measures the regime
body: For material surface areal radius \(R_*\), define compactness \(\mathcal C\coloneqq GM/(R_*c^2)\). Then \(r_s/R_*=2\mathcal C\). Small compactness supports a weak-field surface treatment; approaching the Schwarzschild horizon scale requires fully relativistic reasoning and an appropriate model of the interior or collapse.

title: Escape-speed arithmetic is only a mnemonic
body: Setting the Newtonian escape speed to \(c\) reproduces the same expression, but Newtonian mechanics cannot derive a relativistic causal boundary. The \cref{event horizon}{gr.event_horizon} is established by the metric's causal structure. For rotating or charged black holes the horizon formula changes; \(2GM/c^2\) remains a mass scale rather than their general horizon radius.

title: A boundary defined by escape
body: For an asymptotically flat black-hole spacetime, the future event horizon bounds the region from which no future-directed causal signal can reach future null infinity. It is a global property of the entire causal geometry, not a material surface.

title: The Schwarzschild future horizon
body: In the black-hole extension of Schwarzschild, the future horizon lies at areal radius \(r=2m\). It is a null hypersurface generated by light rays. Outside it some future light rays can escape; on it the outward generators remain on the horizon; inside the black-hole region all future causal paths head to smaller areal radius.

title: Use coordinates that cross the horizon
body: Set \(c\overset{\text{units}}{=}1\). In ingoing coordinates \(v\), the radial metric is \(ds^2=f\,dv^2-2\,dv\,dr\), with \(f=1-2m/r\). Radial null paths obey either \(dv=0\) (ingoing) or \[\frac{dr}{dv}\overset{\text{outgoing null}}{=}\frac{f}{2}.\] The latter derivative is positive outside, zero on the horizon and negative inside. Timelike futures lie between the two null directions, so crossing inward is possible but escaping back out is not.

title: Crossing need not be locally violent
body: The horizon's curvature is finite, and for larger Schwarzschild mass its curvature scale is smaller. A freely falling observer crosses in finite proper time. A stationary observer held just outside instead needs proper acceleration that grows without bound towards the horizon. These are different worldlines, not conflicting descriptions of the same acceleration.

title: A local observation cannot locate a general event horizon
body: The full future is needed to decide which events can send signals to infinity. Local trapped-surface or apparent-horizon criteria are useful but are not the definition used here. In a collapse spacetime, the event horizon need not wait for local curvature to become large. The classical causal argument does not address quantum evaporation.

title: A chart can fail on regular geometry
body: Divergent or degenerate-looking metric components do not by themselves establish a singular spacetime. Coordinates can cease to label events smoothly, as polar coordinates already do at the origin of a flat plane. Schwarzschild's horizon provides a physically consequential example.

title: Build a horizon-crossing chart
body: Use \(c\overset{\text{units}}{=}1\), \(f=1-2m/r\), and define \[r_*\coloneqq r+2m\ln\left|\frac{r}{2m}-1\right|,\qquad v\coloneqq t+r_*.\] Since \(dr_*/dr=1/f\), substituting \(dt=dv-dr/f\) into the Schwarzschild line element gives \[ds^2=f\,dv^2-2\,dv\,dr-r^2d\Omega^2.\] The divergent radial coefficient has cancelled exactly.

title: Check nondegeneracy as well as finiteness
body: The radial components are \(g_{vv}=f\), \(g_{vr}=g_{rv}=-1\), and \(g_{rr}=0\). Their two-dimensional determinant is \(f\cdot0-(-1)^2=-1\), including at \(r=2m\). Thus the metric remains nondegenerate and Lorentzian there. The full determinant is \(-r^4\sin^2\theta\); polar-axis zeros are the familiar angular chart issue.

title: An extension, not a regular old chart
body: The transformation is smooth on its overlap with the exterior chart but singular at that chart's boundary. The resulting ingoing metric extends smoothly across the future horizon, admitting finite tangent components for infalling paths. This demonstrates regularity more strongly than checking a few finite curvature scalars alone.

title: Coordinates cannot remove every singularity
body: At \(r=0\), the Schwarzschild Kretschmann scalar diverges, so no smooth chart change can make the classical curvature regular. Conversely, finite invariants alone are not a universal proof of extendibility. Distinguish chart failure, invariant curvature behaviour and geodesic completeness when diagnosing an apparent boundary.

title: The Schwarzschild interior reaches a geometric boundary
body: In the black-hole region of the classical Schwarzschild solution, decreasing areal radius is unavoidable along future causal motion. The boundary \(r=0\) is a spacelike singularity, not a material point waiting somewhere inside a static spatial cavity.

title: Invariant curvature diverges
body: With \(m\coloneqq GM/c^2\), \[K\coloneqq R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\overset{\text{Schwarzschild}}{=}\frac{48m^2}{r^6}.\] It is finite at \(r=2m\) and diverges as \(r\to0\). Since a regular coordinate change cannot alter this scalar at an event, the central divergence cannot be removed like the horizon's chart failure.

title: A falling observer has finite remaining time
body: For a radial geodesic released from rest at infinity, the exact energy equation gives \(dr/d\tau=-c\sqrt{2m/r}\). Integrating the proper time from horizon to singularity yields \[\Delta\tau\overset{\text{this geodesic}}{=}\frac{1}{c}\int_0^{2m}\sqrt{\frac{r}{2m}}\,dr=\frac{4m}{3c}.\] This value depends on the chosen infall energy; it is not the universal lifetime of every interior observer.

title: Singularity means incomplete classical geometry
body: The singular boundary is not a regular event belonging to the spacetime manifold. In the general theory, singularity statements concern inextendible causal geodesics of finite affine length or proper time; they need not always involve divergent scalar invariants. Schwarzschild has both finite-time incompleteness and divergent curvature.

title: Do not turn breakdown into a microscopic model
body: Classical GR gives no regular matter state at this boundary or account of what replaces it. Quantum gravity may be needed, but a particular resolution is not supplied by the solution. The Schwarzschild spacelike singularity also should not be copied unchanged into rotating or charged black-hole geometries.

title: Use symmetry to reduce radial motion
body: Time-translation and rotational symmetry give constants along Schwarzschild geodesics. Choosing the orbital plane as \(\theta=\pi/2\) reduces the problem to radial motion in an effective potential. The potential is an algebraic aid, not a second gravitational field.

title: Fix the energy normalisation
body: Set \(c\overset{\text{units}}{=}1\), retain \(m\coloneqq GM/c^2\) as a length, and write \(f=1-2m/r\). For timelike motion define \(\mathcal E\coloneqq f\,dt/d\tau\) and \(L\coloneqq r^2d\phi/d\tau\). Here \(\mathcal E\) is energy per unit rest energy and \(L\) is angular momentum per unit rest mass in these units; both are constant along a geodesic.

title: Insert the constants into the norm
body: The proper-time normalisation gives \[1\overset{\text{timelike norm}}{=}f\dot t^2-f^{-1}\dot r^2-r^2\dot\phi^2.\] Multiplication by \(f\) and substitution yield \[\dot r^2+V_{\mathrm{eff}}(r)=\mathcal E^2,\qquad V_{\mathrm{eff}}\coloneqq\left(1-\frac{2m}{r}\right)\left(1+\frac{L^2}{r^2}\right).\] Dots mean proper-time derivatives. Allowed radial motion has \(\mathcal E^2\geq V_{\mathrm{eff}}\), and equality gives a turning point.

title: Circular orbits and stability
body: A circular orbit needs both \(V_{\mathrm{eff}}=\mathcal E^2\) and \(V'_{\mathrm{eff}}=0\) at fixed \(L\). The latter gives \(L^2=mr^2/(r-3m)\). The outer minimum is stable for \(r>6m\); the inner maximum is unstable for \(3m<r<6m\). The limiting orbit at \(r=6m\) is marginally stable, the ISCO. A turning point alone is not a circular orbit.

title: Null geodesics have a different potential
body: For an affine parameter \(\lambda\), define the analogous constants \(\mathcal E=f\,dt/d\lambda\) and \(L=r^2d\phi/d\lambda\). Zero tangent norm gives \(V_{\mathrm{null}}=fL^2/r^2\) and \((dr/d\lambda)^2+V_{\mathrm{null}}=\mathcal E^2\). This potential has a maximum at \(r=3m\), the unstable photon sphere. Null constants change under affine rescaling, but \(b\coloneqq L/\mathcal E\), the asymptotic impact parameter, does not.

title: Einstein's happiest thought
body: In 1907 Einstein realised that an observer falling freely from a roof would not feel their own weight. He later called this insight the happiest thought of his life. The equivalence between free fall and inertial motion gave him a physical route beyond special relativity: gravity might be removed locally by choosing the right state of motion.
statement: Einstein’s 1907 free-fall insight suggested that gravitational effects could disappear locally.

title: From Galileo to Eötvös
body: The empirical seed was the universality of free fall: different bodies accelerate alike when non-gravitational effects are removed. Newton encoded the same fact as equality of inertial and gravitational mass, while Eötvös and later experiments tested that equality with increasing precision. Einstein promoted this numerical coincidence into a principle about all local non-gravitational physics.
statement: Universality of free fall supplied the experimental starting point for Einstein’s broader principle.

title: Why gravity became geometry
body: Einstein's equivalence principle suggested that gravitational acceleration could disappear in a freely falling laboratory, but tidal differences between neighbouring laboratories could not. Riemann's mathematics supplied a language in which geometry is locally flat yet globally curved. By 1915 Einstein had identified the gravitational field with spacetime geometry rather than a force acting within a fixed Euclidean arena.
statement: Einstein combined local free-fall physics with Riemann’s curved geometry in the path to GR.

title: Einstein and Grossmann
body: Einstein did not reach the geometric theory alone. His friend Marcel Grossmann guided him toward the tensor calculus developed by Riemann, Christoffel, Ricci and Levi-Civita, and their 1913 Entwurf theory was an important but incomplete step. The collaboration illustrates how a physical principle and an existing mathematical language had to be brought together before the final field equations were possible.
statement: Grossmann helped connect Einstein’s physical ideas to the existing mathematics of tensor geometry.

title: From Riemann's line element to a gravitational field
body: Riemann's 1854 lecture generalised geometry by allowing the coefficients of a quadratic line element to vary from point to point. Einstein turned that measuring structure into physics: the metric determines clock rates, spatial measurements and light cones while also responding to matter. What had been geometrical data became a dynamical gravitational field.
statement: Riemann’s variable measuring geometry became a dynamical gravitational field in Einstein’s theory.

title: From light cones to global causality
body: Minkowski made light cones central to special-relativistic geometry, but curved spacetime allowed their orientation to vary from event to event. Mid-twentieth-century work by Gödel, Penrose, Hawking and others showed that the global arrangement of cones controls horizons, closed causal curves and singularity theorems. Causality thereby became a subject in its own right rather than a local side-effect of the metric.
statement: Twentieth-century relativity made the global arrangement of light cones central to horizons and causality.

title: Connecting neighbouring tangent spaces
body: Ordinary derivatives silently compare vectors at different points as though all directions belonged to one fixed vector space. Nineteenth-century differential geometry exposed the limitation, and Weyl and Cartan developed the modern idea of an affine connection in the early twentieth century. A connection makes the comparison rule explicit and can therefore describe geometry even before a metric is chosen.
statement: The connection made comparison between neighbouring vector spaces an explicit geometric rule.

title: Christoffel's differential forms
body: Elwin Bruno Christoffel introduced the quantities now called Christoffel symbols in an 1869 study of quadratic differential forms. They were not initially components of a gravitational field; they organised how derivatives change under a change of coordinates. In general relativity the same bookkeeping quantities encode the metric connection, while their ability to vanish at one point warns that they are not themselves curvature.
statement: Christoffel’s 1869 quantities organised differentiation under changes of coordinates before their use in GR.

title: The absolute differential calculus
body: Gregorio Ricci-Curbastro developed methods of invariant differentiation during the late nineteenth century, and with Tullio Levi-Civita presented the absolute differential calculus systematically in 1900. Einstein and Grossmann adopted this machinery because ordinary component derivatives do not transform tensorially in curved coordinates. The covariant derivative became the device that lets local equations retain geometric meaning.
statement: Ricci and Levi-Civita’s calculus supplied derivatives that retain geometric meaning across coordinates.

title: Levi-Civita's distinguished connection
body: For a metric geometry there is a unique connection that preserves the metric and has no torsion: the connection now named for Levi-Civita. Cartan later made torsion an independent geometric object, showing that its absence is a physical and geometric choice rather than part of the definition of every connection. Standard general relativity makes that torsion-free choice.
statement: Cartan distinguished torsion from curvature, making the torsion-free GR choice explicit.

title: Levi-Civita invents parallel transport
body: In 1917 Levi-Civita gave an intrinsic rule for carrying a direction along a curve on a general Riemannian manifold. The construction replaced an ambient-space picture of parallel arrows with one defined entirely inside the geometry. Its path dependence provided an immediate geometric interpretation of curvature and soon became part of the working language of relativity.
statement: Levi-Civita’s intrinsic transport rule gave curvature a direct path-comparison interpretation.

title: From shortest routes to free fall
body: Geodesics began as the shortest or straightest curves on surfaces, studied in geodesy and differential geometry. General relativity changed their physical status: a freely falling test body follows a timelike geodesic, while light follows null geodesics. Gravity was thus shifted from a force bending a trajectory to the geometry that defines what unforced motion means.
statement: GR identified geometrically unforced timelike and null paths with physical free fall and light propagation.

title: Riemann makes curvature intrinsic
body: In his 1854 habilitation lecture Riemann proposed that geometry could vary from place to place and in dimensions beyond ordinary surfaces. The curvature tensor bearing his name packages the obstruction to treating that geometry as flat. Einstein's theory made this abstract nineteenth-century construction observable through tidal gravity and geodesic deviation.

title: Ricci's contraction enters physics
body: The contracted curvature tensor is named for Gregorio Ricci-Curbastro, whose invariant calculus helped organise the geometry inherited by general relativity. Einstein spent years testing curvature combinations that could represent gravitation and source equations. The Ricci tensor became decisive because vacuum gravity can set it to zero while leaving the full Riemann curvature—and therefore tidal gravity—nonzero.

title: The trace term that closes the equation
body: Einstein's route to the final field equations repeatedly approached the Ricci tensor but struggled with covariance and conservation. In November 1915 the trace-adjusted combination now called the Einstein tensor supplied the required divergence-free left-hand side. The extra scalar-curvature term is therefore not cosmetic: it is what lets geometry match local stress-energy conservation.

title: An old identity gains physical force
body: The differential identities bearing Luigi Bianchi's name arose in nineteenth-century geometry, before general relativity. Their contraction implies that the Einstein tensor has zero covariant divergence. Once Einstein's equations tied that tensor to matter, a geometric identity became the consistency condition behind covariant stress-energy conservation.

title: Separating geometry from coordinates
body: Relativity's freedom to change coordinates made component divergences an unreliable guide to physical singularities. Scalar contractions of curvature supplied coordinate-independent tests, with the invariant associated with Erich Kretschmann becoming especially familiar in the Schwarzschild geometry. Such invariants helped distinguish the removable pathology at the horizon from genuine curvature growth at the centre.

title: Einstein, Hilbert and the action
body: David Hilbert presented a variational formulation of gravitation in late 1915 while Einstein was completing the field equations by a different route. Their work was closely timed and historically entangled, but the modern Einstein-Hilbert action should not be read as evidence that one simply supplied the other's theory. Its enduring importance is structural: one scalar action yields the geometric field equations and makes extensions of GR systematic.

title: Assumptions built for global theorems
body: Energy conditions were developed as deliberately broad inequalities rather than detailed models of matter. Raychaudhuri's focusing equation and the singularity theorems of Penrose and Hawking used them to turn local curvature assumptions into global conclusions. Quantum fields can violate several classical energy conditions, so their historical success does not make them inviolable laws of nature.

title: Four weeks in November 1915
body: Einstein presented a sequence of communications to the Prussian Academy in November 1915, revising the gravitational equations almost weekly. On 25 November he gave the generally covariant equations in essentially their modern form. The compressed chronology hides an eight-year search through equivalence, covariance, conservation and the Newtonian limit.

title: Einstein and Hilbert
body: Hilbert submitted an action-based treatment of gravitation within days of Einstein's final academy paper. The surviving record supports independent but interacting routes rather than a simple tale of theft or solitary discovery. Einstein supplied the sustained physical programme and final tensor equation; Hilbert's variational formulation revealed a powerful mathematical organisation of the same theory.

title: Einstein's static universe
body: Einstein introduced the cosmological term in 1917 when applying general relativity to the universe as a whole. He sought a spatially closed, static model, reflecting the limited astronomical evidence then available; without the added term his chosen matter distribution would not remain static. The construction also helped found relativistic cosmology, even though the equilibrium was unstable.

title: From discarded term to dark energy
body: After expanding-universe models and observations displaced the static universe, Einstein no longer favoured his original motivation for the term. The cosmological constant nevertheless remained mathematically legitimate and acquired new interpretations as vacuum energy or dark energy. The discovery of accelerated cosmic expansion in the late 1990s returned it to the centre of cosmology.

title: Einstein predicts gravitational clock shifts
body: Einstein used the equivalence principle in 1907 to argue that gravity must affect clock rates and light frequency. A uniformly accelerating laboratory supplied the thought experiment: light received higher or lower in the cabin has a shifted frequency because the receiver changes velocity during the signal's flight. Reinterpreting acceleration as gravity produced one of the theory's earliest testable consequences.

title: Pound and Rebka measure the shift
body: In 1959–60 Robert Pound and Glen Rebka used the Mössbauer effect to compare gamma rays over the height of Harvard's Jefferson tower. The expected terrestrial shift was extraordinarily small, but recoil-free nuclear resonance made it measurable. Their result turned a once-astronomical relativistic effect into a laboratory measurement and anticipated today's gravitational corrections to precision clocks.

title: From the equivalence principle to the full prediction
body: Einstein predicted solar light bending in 1911 using the equivalence principle, obtaining only half the value of the completed theory. The 1915 field equations added the effect of spatial curvature and doubled the prediction to about 1.75 arcseconds for a ray grazing the Sun. The change is a useful historical warning: equivalence gives local insight but not the complete spacetime geometry.

title: The 1919 eclipse expeditions
body: British expeditions led by Arthur Eddington and Andrew Crommelin photographed stars near the eclipsed Sun in 1919. Their reported deflections favoured Einstein's prediction and made both Einstein and general relativity internationally famous. The measurements were difficult and less decisive than the legend sometimes suggests, but later radio and lensing observations confirmed the relativistic effect with far greater precision.

title: Mercury's unexplained 43 arcseconds
body: Urbain Le Verrier showed in the nineteenth century that known Newtonian perturbations left a small residual advance of Mercury's perihelion. Proposed planets and modifications of gravity failed to settle the anomaly. In November 1915 Einstein obtained the remaining roughly 43 arcseconds per century from his new theory, a result that he regarded as a decisive personal triumph.

title: Einstein's wave prediction
body: Einstein found wave-like weak-field solutions in 1916 and corrected the energy-emission formula in 1918, producing the quadrupole pattern characteristic of gravity. Because coordinate freedom can manufacture apparent ripples, even Einstein later became uncertain about whether exact waves were physical. The episode showed how difficult it was to separate gravitational radiation from coordinate artefacts.

title: Do gravitational waves carry energy?
body: Work by Bondi, Pirani, Robinson and others in the 1950s clarified invariant effects and energy transport by gravitational waves. Feynman's “sticky bead” argument gave a memorable operational test: a passing wave can do work by making beads slide and heat a rod. The reality question was thereby reframed in terms of measurable tidal effects rather than troublesome coordinate components.

title: GW150914
body: On 14 September 2015 the two Advanced LIGO detectors recorded GW150914, a signal from merging stellar-mass black holes. Its evolving waveform matched general-relativistic calculations through inspiral, merger and ringdown. Announced in 2016, it was the first direct detection of gravitational waves and opened gravitational-wave astronomy.

title: Schwarzschild's wartime solution
body: Karl Schwarzschild found the first exact solution of Einstein's field equations only weeks after their final publication, while serving on the Russian front during the First World War. Einstein presented the paper to the Prussian Academy in January 1916. The solution's apparent singular surface later became central to black-hole physics, although that interpretation was not available to Schwarzschild himself.

title: The surface that stopped being singular
body: The radius now called the horizon looked singular in standard Schwarzschild coordinates, encouraging decades of uncertainty about whether it was a physical barrier. Horizon-crossing coordinates developed through work by Eddington, Lemaître and Finkelstein showed that regular infall continues across it. The suspect surface was reinterpreted as a one-way causal boundary rather than a place of divergent curvature.

title: From collapsed stars to black holes
body: Oppenheimer and Snyder modelled continuing stellar collapse in 1939, but relativistic collapsed objects remained marginal for decades. Global causal methods in the 1960s made horizons and trapped surfaces precise, while John Wheeler helped popularise the term “black hole”. The event horizon is the mature geometric concept behind that name, defined by which signals can ever escape.

title: Coordinates created a false obstruction
body: Early discussion often treated the Schwarzschild radius as a singular edge because the original static coordinates fail there. Lemaître's freely falling coordinates and later Eddington-Finkelstein and Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates crossed the surface smoothly. The episode became the standard lesson that divergent metric components diagnose a chart only after invariant geometry has been checked.

title: From ideal collapse to singularity theorems
body: Oppenheimer and Snyder's 1939 model showed that sufficiently massive idealised matter could collapse beyond its Schwarzschild radius, but symmetry left open whether the singular outcome was an artefact. Penrose's 1965 theorem used trapped surfaces and global causality to show that geodesic incompleteness is a robust prediction under broad conditions. Singularity became a statement about the limits of classical spacetime, not merely an infinite number in special coordinates.
